quiz.explain: f maps each x to itself, so range = R and f(0) = 0.
steps: f(x) = x sends each x to itself
So every real number is an output: range = R
f(0) = 0, so the graph y = x passes through the origin
Answer: Its range is R and its graph passes through the origin
quiz.mistake: Confuses identity function with constant function 1

quiz.q: The range of f(x) = x², x ∈ R, is:
quiz.explain: Squares are never negative and 0 = 0² is attained.
steps: Every non-negative number is a square (e.g. 9 = 3²)
quiz.mistake: Excludes 0 or allows negative squares

quiz.q: For f(x) = 1/x, what is f(1/4) − f(4)?
quiz.explain: f(1/4) = 4 and f(4) = 1/4, so the difference is 4 − 1/4 = 15/4.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts in the wrong order or adds

teach.ask: Gappu must sketch y = x, y = 3, y = x², y = x³ and y = 1/x for a test. Explain what each graph looks like and its range.
teach.praise: Line, flat line, U, S-curve and two branches. My sketchbook is ready!
teach.nudge: Which of these graphs never touches either axis?

revise.summary: Common real functions: identity f(x) = x (range R), constant f(x) = c (range {c}), polynomials such as x² and x³, rational functions p(x)/q(x) defined where q(x) ≠ 0, and 1/x with domain and range R − {0}.
focus: Identify polynomial and rational functions
Find the domain of a rational function by removing zeros of the denominator
Know the graphs and ranges of x, c, x², x³ and 1/x
Evaluate these functions at given points
remember: Identity f(x) = x: domain and range R; constant f(x) = c: range {c}
Polynomial: a₀ + a₁x + … + aₙxⁿ, n a non-negative integer; x² has range [0, ∞), x³ has range R
Rational function f(x)/g(x) is defined where g(x) ≠ 0
y = 1/x: domain and range R − {0}; graph in quadrants I and III
traps: 1/x has a negative power (x⁻¹), so x² + 1/x is not a polynomial
Only zeros of the denominator are removed from the domain, not zeros of the numerator

topics.title: Modulus, signum and greatest integer functions

learn.hook: Distance never goes negative, a cricket umpire's signal is 'out, not out or wait', and a parking lot charges for every started hour. Meet |x|, signum and [x].
points: Modulus: |x| = x if x ≥ 0 and −x if x < 0. Domain R, range [0, ∞); graph is a V with vertex at the origin.
Signum: f(x) = 1 if x > 0, 0 if x = 0, −1 if x < 0 (equal to |x|/x for x ≠ 0). Domain R, range {−1, 0, 1}.
Greatest integer function [x]: the greatest integer less than or equal to x. [2.7] = 2, [−2.7] = −3, [5] = 5.
[x] has domain R and range Z; its graph is a staircase with a filled dot at the left end of each step and a hollow dot at the right.
For −1 ≤ x < 0, [x] = −1; for 0 ≤ x < 1, [x] = 0; and so on.
learn.reallife: Indian Railways' fare table rounds a journey of 251–300 km into one slab — that is a step function just like [x].

games.title: Special function facts
items: |x| ≥ 0 and every non-negative value is attained.
−1 is greater than −1.5; the greatest integer ≤ −1.5 is −2.
The range of the signum function is {−1, 0, 1}.
Those are its only three outputs.
The graph of |x| is a V shape with vertex at (0, 0).
Two rays y = x and y = −x meeting at the origin.
An integer is the greatest integer not exceeding itself.
The domain of the greatest integer function is Z.
Its domain is R; its range is Z.

quiz.q: What is [−4.2]?
quiz.explain: −5 ≤ −4.2 < −4, so the greatest integer not exceeding −4.2 is −5.
steps: −4 is bigger than −4.2, so it is not allowed
quiz.mistake: Simply drops the decimal part, giving −4

quiz.q: The range of the signum function is:
quiz.explain: The function takes only the values −1 (x < 0), 0 (x = 0) and 1 (x > 0).
steps: Signum takes the value 1 for x > 0, 0 for x = 0 and −1 for x < 0
No other value is ever produced
So the range is the set of these three numbers
quiz.mistake: Forgets the value 0 at x = 0

quiz.q: For x < 0, |x| equals:
quiz.explain: If x is negative, −x is positive, and that is the distance from 0.
steps: Definition: |x| = x for x ≥ 0, and −x for x < 0
For negative x, −x is positive, e.g. x = −5 gives −x = 5
That is the distance of x from 0
quiz.mistake: Thinks |x| = x always
Takes [−2.5] = −2 and gets 0

quiz.q: Which value of x gives [x] = 3?
quiz.explain: 3 ≤ x < 4 gives [x] = 3. 3.99 lies in this interval; 4 gives 4 and 2.99 gives 2.
quiz.mistake: Includes the right end point 4

quiz.q: f(x) = |x|/x for x ≠ 0. What is f(−3)?
quiz.explain: |−3|/(−3) = 3/(−3) = −1. This is the signum function for x ≠ 0.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the denominator is negative

quiz.q: Which statement about the graph of y = [x] is true?
options: It is a straight line through the origin
On [1, 2) it is the horizontal segment y = 1 with a filled dot at x = 1 and a hollow dot at x = 2
quiz.explain: [x] is constant on each interval [n, n + 1), so the graph is a staircase.
steps: On [1, 2): [x] = 1, a horizontal segment at y = 1
x = 1 is included (filled dot); at x = 2 the value jumps to 2 (hollow dot)
Horizontal segment y = 1 on [1, 2), filled dot at x = 1, hollow dot at x = 2
Answer: On [1, 2) it is the horizontal segment y = 1 with a filled dot at x = 1 and a hollow dot at x = 2
quiz.mistake: Confuses [x] with x or |x|

quiz.q: How many integer values of x satisfy |x| < 3?
quiz.mistake: Includes ±3

teach.ask: Gappu thinks [−2.5] = −2 and that |x| is always just x. Teach Gappu the modulus, signum and greatest integer functions.
teach.praise: So [−2.5] is −3 — step DOWN, not towards zero. Mind officially blown!
teach.nudge: For a negative number like −2.5, is the greatest integer below it −2 or −3?

revise.summary: The modulus |x| gives the distance from 0, the signum function gives 1, 0 or −1 by the sign of x, and the greatest integer function [x] gives the greatest integer ≤ x, with range Z.
focus: Evaluate |x|, signum x and [x], especially for negative numbers
State domain and range: |x| → [0, ∞), signum → {−1, 0, 1}, [x] → Z
Describe the graphs: V shape for |x|, staircase for [x]
Solve simple conditions like [x] = 3 or |x| < 3
remember: |x| = x if x ≥ 0, and −x if x < 0
Signum: 1 if x > 0, 0 if x = 0, −1 if x < 0; equals |x|/x for x ≠ 0
[x] = n for n ≤ x < n + 1
traps: [−4.2] is −5, not −4: go down to the integer on the left
The signum range is {−1, 0, 1}, not the interval [−1, 1]

learn.hook: A startup's profit is revenue minus cost: P(x) = R(x) − C(x). Adding, subtracting and dividing functions is everyday business maths.
points: (f + g)(x) = f(x) + g(x) and (f − g)(x) = f(x) − g(x), on the common domain D_f ∩ D_g.
(fg)(x) = f(x)·g(x) on D_f ∩ D_g; (αf)(x) = α f(x) for a real constant α.
(f/g)(x) = f(x)/g(x) on D_f ∩ D_g, excluding points where g(x) = 0.
Piecewise functions use different rules on different intervals; check that overlapping pieces agree.
Difference quotient: [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h. For f(x) = x², [f(1.1) − f(1)]/(1.1 − 1) = 0.21/0.1 = 2.1.

example.q: f(x) = √x and g(x) = x are defined on non-negative reals. Find (f + g)(x), (fg)(x) and (f/g)(x) with domains.
steps: f/g = √x/x = 1/√x, but g(0) = 0, so exclude x = 0.

learn.reallife: A Mumbai dabbawala's daily earning E(x) = 20x − 150 (₹20 per tiffin, ₹150 fixed cost) is a linear function found from two data points.

games.title: Find the domain of f/g for f(x) = √(x − 1), g(x) = x − 4
items: g is defined for all real x, so the common domain is [1, ∞)

steps: Both f and g are defined for all real x
quiz.mistake: Excludes the zero of f instead of g

Not a function: at x = 2 the rules give 4 and 6

teach.ask: Gappu wants to divide one function by another. Explain how to add, multiply and divide real functions and how to get the domain.

teach.nudge: When you form f/g, which extra points must you throw out of the domain?

focus: Compute (f ± g)(a), (fg)(a), (αf)(a) and (f/g)(a)
Find the domain of f/g by removing zeros of g
Check whether a piecewise rule is a well-defined function
Find a linear function from two values
remember: (f ± g)(x) = f(x) ± g(x) and (fg)(x) = f(x)·g(x) on D_f ∩ D_g
(f/g)(x) = f(x)/g(x) on D_f ∩ D_g, excluding g(x) = 0
(αf)(x) = α f(x)

Overlapping pieces of a piecewise rule must give the same value, or it is not a function

topics.title: Angles as rotation: degrees and radians

learn.hook: A ceiling fan blade, a Ferris wheel at a Dussehra mela and the hands of a clock all sweep angles far bigger than 90° — so trigonometry must grow up beyond right triangles.
points: In Class 10, trigonometric ratios were defined for acute angles. Now we extend them to angles of any size, and then to any real number.
An angle is the amount of rotation of a ray from its initial side to its terminal side. Anticlockwise rotation gives a positive angle; clockwise gives a negative one.
Degree measure: one full turn = 360°; 1° = 60′ (minutes), 1′ = 60″ (seconds).
Radian measure: the angle at the centre subtended by an arc whose length equals the radius is 1 radian. In general θ = l/r (θ in radians).
Convention: when no unit is written, the angle is in radians. So 'sin 2' means the sine of 2 radians, and θ = π/3 means π/3 radians.

example.q: An arc of length 18 cm subtends an angle θ at the centre of a circle of radius 6 cm. Find θ.
steps: Use θ = l/r with l = 18 cm and r = 6 cm.

learn.reallife: An ISRO antenna turning 'through 2 radians' and a cricket ball spinning several full turns both use rotation measure that can exceed 360°.

games.title: Angle basics
items: An angle can be greater than 360°.
More than one full rotation is allowed, e.g. 450°.
A clockwise rotation gives a positive angle.
By convention anticlockwise is positive, clockwise is negative.
θ = l/r gives θ in degrees.
θ = l/r gives the angle in radians.
If an angle is written without units, it is taken in radians.
Degrees split into minutes, minutes into seconds.
1 radian is the angle of an arc equal to the diameter.
It is the angle of an arc equal to the radius.

quiz.q: An arc of length 12 cm subtends an angle of 1.5 radians at the centre. What is the radius?
quiz.mistake: Multiplies l by θ instead of dividing

quiz.q: A circle has radius 10 cm. What arc length subtends an angle of 2.5 radians?
quiz.mistake: Divides r by θ

quiz.q: How many seconds (″) are there in 1°?
quiz.mistake: Stops at 60 minutes

quiz.q: A ray rotates three-quarters of a full turn clockwise. The angle formed is:
quiz.explain: Three-quarters of 360° is 270°; clockwise makes it negative.
steps: Clockwise rotation gives a negative angle
quiz.mistake: Ignores the direction of rotation

quiz.q: In the statement 'sin 1 > 0', the angle 1 is measured in:
quiz.explain: Angles written without units are radians by convention.
steps: Convention: when no unit is written, the angle is in radians
The angle is measured in radians
quiz.mistake: Assumes degrees whenever no unit is shown

quiz.q: Which angle is the same as 1 full revolution plus a quarter turn anticlockwise?
quiz.explain: 360° + 90° = 450°, positive because anticlockwise.
steps: Anticlockwise, so the angle is positive
quiz.mistake: Forgets the full revolution

quiz.q: Why do we need trigonometric functions of angles larger than 90°?
options: Rotations such as wheels and clock hands go beyond a right angle, and right-triangle ratios only cover acute angles
Acute angles do not have trigonometric ratios
Radians only work for obtuse angles
quiz.explain: Right triangles only give ratios for 0° < θ < 90°. Defining functions for any angle lets us describe all rotations and periodic motion.
steps: Right-triangle ratios only work for acute angles, 0° < θ < 90°
Wheels and clock hands keep rotating far beyond 90°
To describe all rotations we need trig functions for any angle
So: rotations go beyond a right angle, and right-triangle ratios only cover acute angles
Answer: Rotations such as wheels and clock hands go beyond a right angle, and right-triangle ratios only cover acute angles
quiz.mistake: Thinks trigonometry is only about triangles

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): An angle of 2 radians is larger than a right angle.
Reason (R): 1 radian is about 57°16′.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: 2 radians ≈ 114°32′, which is more than 90°. R gives the size of 1 radian, which explains A.
steps: A follows directly from the size of 1 radian in R
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Treats 2 radians as 2°

teach.ask: Gappu says 'angles are just triangles' corners, between 0° and 90°'. Explain angles as rotation, and what a radian is.
teach.praise: So a radian is an arc as long as the radius, and angles can keep spinning past 360°!
teach.nudge: What exactly is 1 radian — which length equals which?

revise.summary: An angle measures the rotation of a ray from its initial to its terminal side: anticlockwise is positive, clockwise negative. It is measured in degrees (360° per turn) or radians, where θ = l/r.
focus: Give the sign of an angle from the direction of rotation
Use θ = l/r (θ in radians) to find an angle or an arc length
Convert between degrees, minutes and seconds
Read angles with no unit as radians
remember: Anticlockwise rotation: positive angle; clockwise: negative angle
1 radian: angle subtended at the centre by an arc equal to the radius; θ = l/r
No unit written → the angle is in radians
traps: Don't read 'sin 2' as sin 2°: it means 2 radians
Don't use θ in degrees in l = rθ

topics.title: Converting degrees and radians; arc problems

learn.hook: A Ferris wheel turning 540 times a minute? That's a centrifuge! Converting revolutions, degrees and radians is daily work for engineers.
points: A full circle is 2π radians = 360°, so π radians = 180°.
Degrees → radians: multiply by π/180. Radians → degrees: multiply by 180/π.
1 radian = 180°/π ≈ 57°16′ (approx.) and 1° = π/180 ≈ 0.01746 radian (approx.).
For degree–minute form, first change minutes to degrees: 47°30′ = 47.5° = 95/2 degrees.
Arc problems use l = rθ (θ in radians). One revolution = 2π radians; when a number is needed, NCERT often uses π = 22/7.

example.q: Convert −47°30′ into radians.

learn.reallife: A Mumbai local's wheel of radius 0.5 m that turns through 2π radians moves the train 2π × 0.5 ≈ 3.14 m — arc length is distance travelled.

quiz.q: A wheel makes 360 revolutions in one minute. Through how many radians does it turn in one second?
quiz.explain: 360 rev/min = 6 rev/s. Each revolution is 2π, so 6 × 2π = 12π radians.
steps: 360 revolutions per minute ÷ 60 = 6 revolutions per second
The wheel turns 12π radians in one second
quiz.mistake: Forgets to convert minutes to seconds, or uses π per revolution

quiz.q: Convert 5π/3 radians to degrees.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies by π/180 instead of 180/π

quiz.q: A pendulum 60 cm long swings so that its tip moves along an arc of 15 cm. The angle of swing in radians is:
quiz.explain: θ = l/r = 15/60 = 1/4 radian.
steps: Given: r = 60 cm, arc l = 15 cm
quiz.mistake: Divides r by l

quiz.q: Find the length of the minor arc of a circle of radius 21 cm cut off by a chord equal to the radius. (Use π = 22/7.)
quiz.explain: A chord equal to the radius makes an equilateral triangle, so the angle is 60° = π/3. Arc = 21 × π/3 = 7π = 22 cm.
quiz.mistake: Takes the arc as equal to the chord

quiz.q: Arcs of the same length in two circles subtend 45° and 60° at their centres. Find the ratio r₁ : r₂.
quiz.explain: l = r₁(π/4) = r₂(π/3) gives r₁/r₂ = (π/3)/(π/4) = 4/3.
steps: Same arc l in both circles: l = r₁θ₁ = r₂θ₂
quiz.mistake: Thinks bigger angle means bigger radius

quiz.q: Convert 40°20′ to radians.
Using π = 22/7, convert 11/16 radian to degrees.
quiz.mistake: Stops at decimal minutes or rounds too early

quiz.q: The minute hand of a clock is 1.5 cm long. How far does its tip move in 40 minutes? (Use π = 3.14.)
quiz.explain: In 40 minutes the hand turns 40/60 × 360° = 240° = 4π/3. Distance = 1.5 × 4π/3 = 2π = 6.28 cm.
quiz.mistake: Uses 40° instead of 240°

teach.ask: Gappu needs to change 135° to radians and back. Explain the rule connecting degrees and radians and how to find an arc length.
teach.praise: π radians = 180°, and arc = radius × angle. Converting is a breeze now!
teach.nudge: What is π radians equal to in degrees?

revise.summary: Since π radians = 180°, multiply by π/180 to change degrees to radians and by 180/π to change radians to degrees. Arc problems use l = rθ with θ in radians.
focus: Convert degrees (including minutes) to radians and radians to degrees
Solve arc, pendulum and wheel problems with l = rθ
Turn revolutions into radians using 1 revolution = 2π
remember: π radians = 180°; 2π radians = 360°
Degrees → radians: × π/180; radians → degrees: × 180/π
traps: Change minutes to degrees before converting: 47°30′ = 47.5°, not 47.30°
Don't forget that one revolution is 2π radians, not π

topics.title: Trigonometric functions on the unit circle

learn.hook: Watch a point riding a circle of radius 1 — its x-coordinate is cos x and its y-coordinate is sin x. Every trig fact follows from that one picture.
points: Take the unit circle centred at O. If the arc from (1, 0) to P has length x (radians), then P = (cos x, sin x). Since P is on the circle, cos²x + sin²x = 1.
tan x = sin x/cos x (cos x ≠ 0), cot x = cos x/sin x (sin x ≠ 0), sec x = 1/cos x, cosec x = 1/sin x.
Quadrantal values: sin 0 = 0, sin π/2 = 1, sin π = 0, sin 3π/2 = −1, sin 2π = 0; cos 0 = 1, cos π/2 = 0, cos π = −1, cos 3π/2 = 0, cos 2π = 1.
sin x = 0 exactly when x = nπ; cos x = 0 exactly when x = (2n + 1)π/2, where n is any integer.
Dividing cos²x + sin²x = 1 by cos²x or sin²x: 1 + tan²x = sec²x and 1 + cot²x = cosec²x.

example.q: Find the value of sin²(π/4) + cos²(π/6) − tan²(π/3).

learn.reallife: Sound engineers at AIR model a pure tone as y = sin(ωt): the up-and-down motion of a point going round a circle.

quiz.q: What is the value of sin(3π/2) + cos(π)?
quiz.explain: sin(3π/2) = −1 and cos π = −1, so the sum is −2.
steps: cos π = −1 (left end of the circle)
quiz.mistake: Takes sin(3π/2) as +1

quiz.q: On the unit circle, the point reached after an arc of length x from (1, 0) is:
quiz.explain: The x-coordinate is cos x and the y-coordinate is sin x.
steps: On the unit circle, a point is (x-coordinate, y-coordinate)
The x-coordinate is cos x and the y-coordinate is sin x
So the point is (cos x, sin x)
quiz.mistake: Swaps sine and cosine

quiz.q: Find 2 cos²(π/4) + cosec²(7π/6) sin²(π/6).
quiz.explain: cos(π/4) = 1/√2 gives 2 × 1/2 = 1. cosec(7π/6) = −2 so cosec² = 4; sin²(π/6) = 1/4, product 1. Total 2.
quiz.mistake: Takes cosec(7π/6) = −1/2

quiz.q: For which values of x is cos x = 0?
quiz.explain: cos x is the x-coordinate, which is 0 at the top and bottom of the unit circle: odd multiples of π/2.
steps: cos x is the x-coordinate of the point on the unit circle
x-coordinate = 0 at the top (π/2) and bottom (3π/2), and every π after that
These are the odd multiples of π/2
cos x = 0 at x = (2n + 1)π/2, n ∈ Z
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the zeros of sin and cos

quiz.q: If sec x = 13/12, what is tan²x?
steps: Identity: 1 + tan²x = sec²x, so tan²x = sec²x − 1
quiz.mistake: Adds 1 instead of subtracting

quiz.q: tan x is NOT defined when:
quiz.explain: tan x = sin x/cos x, so it fails when cos x = 0, i.e. at odd multiples of π/2.
steps: A fraction is undefined when its denominator is 0
So tan x fails exactly when cos x = 0 (odd multiples of π/2)
tan x is not defined when cos x = 0
quiz.mistake: Confuses tan with cot

quiz.q: What is the value of cot²(π/4) + cosec(5π/6) + 3 tan²(π/3)?
quiz.mistake: Takes cosec(5π/6) as negative, getting 8

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): sin²x + cos²x = 1 for every real x.
Reason (R): (cos x, sin x) lies on the circle x² + y² = 1.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Because P = (cos x, sin x) is on the unit circle, its coordinates satisfy x² + y² = 1. R explains A exactly.
steps: R: P = (cos x, sin x) lies on the unit circle x² + y² = 1, which is true
Substituting the coordinates: cos²x + sin²x = 1, which is A
So A is true, and it follows directly from R
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Thinks the identity only holds for acute angles

teach.ask: Gappu only knows sin as 'opposite over hypotenuse'. Explain how the unit circle defines sin x and cos x for every real x.
teach.praise: A point going round a circle: x is cos, y is sin. Simple and beautiful!
teach.nudge: On the unit circle, which coordinate gives cos x and which gives sin x?

revise.summary: On the unit circle, the point reached by an arc of length x from (1, 0) is (cos x, sin x), so cos²x + sin²x = 1. The other four functions are ratios or reciprocals of sin and cos.
focus: Read sin x and cos x as the coordinates of a point on the unit circle
Recall sin and cos at 0, π/2, π, 3π/2 and 2π
Find where sin x = 0, cos x = 0, and where tan, sec, cot and cosec are undefined
Use 1 + tan²x = sec²x and 1 + cot²x = cosec²x
remember: P = (cos x, sin x) on the unit circle; cos²x + sin²x = 1
tan x = sin x/cos x, cot x = cos x/sin x, sec x = 1/cos x, cosec x = 1/sin x
sin x = 0 when x = nπ; cos x = 0 when x = (2n + 1)π/2
1 + tan²x = sec²x and 1 + cot²x = cosec²x
traps: The point is (cos x, sin x), not (sin x, cos x): cos is the x-coordinate
tan x is undefined where cos x = 0, not where sin x = 0

topics.title: Signs in the quadrants; finding all values from one

learn.hook: Know one trig value and the quadrant, and you can unlock all six — like knowing a locker code and the floor number.
points: Quadrant I (0 to π/2): all six functions positive.
Quadrant II (π/2 to π): only sin and cosec positive.
Quadrant III (π to 3π/2): only tan and cot positive.
Quadrant IV (3π/2 to 2π): only cos and sec positive.
Method: use sin²x + cos²x = 1 (or 1 + tan²x = sec²x) to find the size, then fix the sign from the quadrant.

example.q: If cos x = −12/13 and x lies in the third quadrant, find the other five trigonometric functions.
steps: In quadrant III, sin x < 0, so sin x = −5/13.
example.answer: sin x = −5/13, tan x = 5/12, cot x = 12/5, sec x = −13/12, cosec x = −13/5

learn.reallife: Navigators reading a compass bearing in the second quadrant know at once that the east–west component (cos) is negative — signs carry direction.

games.title: Sign check
items: 200° is in quadrant III, where sin is negative.
100° is in quadrant II, where cos is negative.
300° is in quadrant IV where cos, and hence sec, is positive.
150° is in quadrant II, where sin and cosec are positive.

quiz.q: If sin x = 3/5 and x lies in the second quadrant, then cos x is:
quiz.explain: cos²x = 1 − 9/25 = 16/25, and cos x < 0 in quadrant II, so cos x = −4/5.
steps: In quadrant II, cos x is negative
quiz.mistake: Keeps the positive square root regardless of quadrant

quiz.q: If tan x = −5/12 and x lies in the fourth quadrant, then sec x is:
quiz.explain: sec²x = 1 + 25/144 = 169/144. In quadrant IV cos x > 0, so sec x = 13/12.
steps: In quadrant IV, cos x > 0, so sec x > 0
quiz.mistake: Copies the negative sign of tan onto sec

quiz.q: If cot x = 3/4 and x lies in the third quadrant, then sin x is:
quiz.explain: cosec²x = 1 + 9/16 = 25/16, cosec x = −5/4 in quadrant III, so sin x = −4/5.
steps: In quadrant III, sin x < 0, so cosec x = −5/4
quiz.mistake: Picks the cosine value instead of sine

quiz.q: In which quadrant are both sin x and tan x negative?
quiz.explain: In quadrant IV, sin < 0 and cos > 0, so tan < 0 too. In II tan < 0 but sin > 0; in III tan > 0.
steps: Quadrant I: both positive; II: sin > 0, tan < 0
IV: sin < 0 and cos > 0, so tan = sin/cos < 0
Both negative in the fourth quadrant
quiz.mistake: Thinks negative sin always means quadrant III

quiz.q: If sec x = 13/5 and x lies in the fourth quadrant, then tan x is:
quiz.explain: tan²x = sec²x − 1 = 144/25, and tan < 0 in quadrant IV, so tan x = −12/5.
steps: In quadrant IV, tan x is negative
quiz.mistake: Forgets the sign rule for quadrant IV

quiz.q: If cos x = −1/2 and x lies in the third quadrant, then tan x is:
quiz.explain: sin x = −√3/2 in quadrant III, so tan x = (−√3/2)/(−1/2) = √3.
steps: sin²x = 1 − 1/4 = 3/4, so |sin x| = √3/2; in quadrant III sin x < 0 → sin x = −√3/2
quiz.mistake: Makes tan negative because cos is negative

quiz.q: If cosec x = −41/9 and x lies in the fourth quadrant, then cos x is:
quiz.explain: sin x = −9/41, cos²x = 1 − 81/1681 = 1600/1681, and cos > 0 in quadrant IV, so cos x = 40/41.
quiz.mistake: Uses the sign of cosec for cos

quiz.q: Which function is positive in quadrant III?
quiz.explain: In quadrant III, sin and cos are both negative, so their ratios tan and cot are positive.
steps: In quadrant III, sin x < 0 and cos x < 0
So sec x, cos x and sin x are all negative there
cot x is positive in quadrant III
quiz.mistake: Assumes everything is negative in quadrant III

teach.ask: Gappu knows cos x = −12/13 but can't decide whether sin x is +5/13 or −5/13. Explain how the quadrant decides the sign.
teach.praise: Use the identity for the size, the quadrant for the sign. Locker unlocked!
teach.nudge: Which quadrant are we in, and which functions are positive there?

revise.summary: The signs of the trig functions depend on the quadrant: all positive in I, only sin and cosec in II, only tan and cot in III, only cos and sec in IV. Find the size from an identity, then fix the sign.
focus: Recall which functions are positive in each quadrant
Find all six trig values from one value and the quadrant
Use sin²x + cos²x = 1, 1 + tan²x = sec²x and 1 + cot²x = cosec²x for the size
remember: Quadrant I: all positive; II: sin, cosec positive
Quadrant III: tan, cot positive; IV: cos, sec positive
Method: find the size from an identity, then choose the sign from the quadrant
traps: Don't drop the sign: the square root gives only the size
In quadrant III both sin and cos are negative, so tan and cot are positive

learn.hook: The monsoon returns every year, a pendulum every few seconds, and sin x every 2π. Periodicity lets you tame angles like 765° in one step.
points: sin and cos: domain R, range [−1, 1]. tan: domain R − {(2n + 1)π/2}, range R. cot: domain R − {nπ}, range R.
sec: domain R − {(2n + 1)π/2}; cosec: domain R − {nπ}. Both have range R − (−1, 1), i.e. |y| ≥ 1.
sin(2nπ + x) = sin x and cos(2nπ + x) = cos x: period 2π. tan(nπ + x) = tan x and cot(nπ + x) = cot x: period π.
Large angles: remove whole turns (multiples of 360° or 2π) first. sin 765° = sin(720° + 45°) = sin 45° = 1/√2.
Negative angles: cos(−x) = cos x and sin(−x) = −sin x. So cos(−1710°) = cos 1710° = cos(4 × 360° + 270°) = cos 270° = 0.

example.q: Find sec(−1380°).

learn.reallife: The tides at Mumbai's coast follow an approximately periodic pattern, so planners model them with sine curves.

games.title: Match the function to its range
pairs: Range R; undefined at odd multiples of π/2
Range R; undefined at multiples of π

quiz.q: What is the value of tan(25π/3)?
quiz.explain: 25π/3 = 8π + π/3, and tan has period π, so tan(25π/3) = tan(π/3) = √3.
steps: tan has period π, so tan(8π + π/3) = tan(π/3)
quiz.mistake: Removes only 2π at a time and makes an arithmetic slip

quiz.q: What is sin(−17π/3)?
quiz.mistake: Uses sin(−x) = −sin x but then reduces 17π/3 wrongly

quiz.q: The range of cos x is:
quiz.explain: cos x is the x-coordinate of a point on the unit circle, so it lies between −1 and 1 inclusive.
steps: cos x is the x-coordinate of a point on the unit circle
So −1 ≤ cos x ≤ 1, with cos 0 = 1 and cos π = −1 reached
quiz.mistake: Thinks cos x is never negative

quiz.q: The domain of tan x is:
quiz.explain: tan x = sin x/cos x is undefined where cos x = 0, i.e. at odd multiples of π/2.
steps: tan x = sin x/cos x needs cos x ≠ 0
quiz.mistake: Uses the zeros of sin instead of cos

quiz.q: What is cot(−19π/4)?
quiz.explain: −19π/4 + 5π = π/4, and cot has period π, so the value is cot(π/4) = 1.
steps: cot has period π, so add 5π = 20π/4
quiz.mistake: Applies cot(−x) = −cot x without reducing, getting −1

quiz.q: Which value can sec x NEVER take?
quiz.explain: sec x = 1/cos x and |cos x| ≤ 1, so |sec x| ≥ 1. 1/2 is impossible.
steps: sec x = 1/cos x and −1 ≤ cos x ≤ 1
So |sec x| ≥ 1: sec x ≥ 1 or sec x ≤ −1
−3, 2 and −1 are allowed; 1/2 lies between −1 and 1
quiz.mistake: Thinks sec x has the same range as cos x

quiz.q: What is the period of tan x?
quiz.explain: tan(x + π) = tan x for all x in its domain, and no smaller positive number works.
steps: tan(x + π) = tan x for all x in the domain
No smaller positive number does this (π/2 makes tan undefined)
So the smallest repeat length is π
quiz.mistake: Assumes all trig functions have period 2π

quiz.q: Evaluate cos 1830°.
quiz.mistake: Reduces by 360° one time too many or too few

teach.ask: Gappu panics at 'sin 765°'. Explain what periodicity means and how to reduce big or negative angles.
teach.praise: 765° is just 45° after two full spins. Big angles don't scare me now!
teach.nudge: After how many degrees do sin and cos repeat their values?

revise.summary: sin and cos have domain R and range [−1, 1]; tan and sec exclude odd multiples of π/2, cot and cosec exclude multiples of π. sin and cos repeat every 2π, tan and cot every π.
focus: State the domain and range of all six trig functions
Reduce large angles by removing whole turns (360° or 2π)
Handle negative angles with cos(−x) = cos x and sin(−x) = −sin x
Use period π for tan and cot
remember: sin, cos: domain R, range [−1, 1]; tan: domain R − {(2n + 1)π/2}, range R
sec and cosec: range R − (−1, 1), i.e. |y| ≥ 1
Period of sin and cos: 2π; period of tan and cot: π
cos(−x) = cos x; sin(−x) = −sin x
traps: The range of cos x includes −1 and 1: it is [−1, 1], not (−1, 1)
sec x can never be a number between −1 and 1, such as 1/2

learn.hook: ECG waves at AIIMS, AC current in your home, and ocean waves — all look like the graph of sin x. Let's read those curves.
points: sin x: increases from 0 to 1 in quadrant I, decreases from 1 to 0 in II, decreases from 0 to −1 in III, increases from −1 to 0 in IV.
cos x: decreases from 1 to 0 in I and from 0 to −1 in II; increases from −1 to 0 in III and from 0 to 1 in IV.
tan x: increases in every quadrant — from 0 to ∞ in I, −∞ to 0 in II, 0 to ∞ in III and −∞ to 0 in IV — with vertical asymptotes at odd multiples of π/2.
Graphs of sin and cos are waves between −1 and 1 with period 2π; the cos graph is the sin graph shifted left by π/2.
cot has asymptotes at x = nπ; sec has asymptotes where cos x = 0 and cosec where sin x = 0, and their graphs never enter the band −1 < y < 1.

example.q: In which quadrants are both sin x and cos x decreasing?
steps: sin decreases in quadrants II and III.
cos decreases in quadrants I and II.
example.answer: Only in the second quadrant (π/2 < x < π)

learn.reallife: Household AC supply in India is 230 V at 50 Hz: the voltage traces a sine wave 50 times every second.

games.title: Match the graph feature
pairs: Asymptotes at odd multiples of π/2

quiz.q: In which quadrant does cos x increase from −1 to 0?
quiz.explain: At x = π, cos x = −1; at x = 3π/2, cos x = 0. That stretch is quadrant III.
steps: So cos x rises from −1 to 0 between π and 3π/2
quiz.mistake: Thinks cos only increases in quadrant I

quiz.q: The graph of y = sin x crosses the x-axis at:
quiz.explain: The zeros of sin x are exactly the integer multiples of π.
steps: y = sin x crosses the x-axis where sin x = 0
sin x = 0 exactly when x = nπ
(2n + 1)π/2 are the zeros of cos, not sin
quiz.mistake: Uses the zeros of cos x

quiz.q: Which is true about tan x in quadrant II?
quiz.explain: Just after π/2, tan x is a very large negative number, and it rises to 0 at π.
steps: Just after π/2, cos x is a tiny negative number and sin x ≈ 1, so tan x is a huge negative number
tan x increases in every quadrant
In quadrant II tan x increases from −∞ to 0
quiz.mistake: Thinks negative values must be decreasing

quiz.q: The maximum value of y = sin x is reached at:
quiz.explain: sin x = 1 at the top of the unit circle, x = π/2, and every 2π after that.
steps: sin x = 1 at the top of the unit circle, x = π/2
quiz.mistake: Confuses with the maximum of cos x at x = 0

quiz.q: Which graph has NO points with −1 < y < 1?
quiz.explain: |sec x| = 1/|cos x| ≥ 1, so the graph avoids that band. tan and cot take every real value.
steps: So |sec x| ≥ 1, and its graph never enters −1 < y < 1
sin x stays inside [−1, 1]; tan and cot take every real value
y = sec x has no points with −1 < y < 1
quiz.mistake: Thinks tan has the same range as sec

quiz.q: The graph of y = cos x can be obtained from y = sin x by:
options: shifting it π/2 to the left
shifting it π to the right
quiz.explain: cos x = sin(x + π/2), which is the sin graph moved left by π/2.
steps: Replacing x by x + π/2 moves a graph π/2 to the left
So the cos graph is the sin graph shifted left
Shift y = sin x by π/2 to the left
Answer: shifting it π/2 to the left
quiz.mistake: Uses the wrong direction or a full π shift

quiz.q: How many times does the graph of y = sin x cut the x-axis for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π?
quiz.explain: It cuts at x = 0, π and 2π.
steps: y = sin x cuts the x-axis where sin x = 0, i.e. x = nπ
quiz.mistake: Leaves out one of the end points

quiz.q: Where does y = tan x have vertical asymptotes?
quiz.explain: tan x is undefined where cos x = 0, and the graph shoots off to ±∞ near those lines.
steps: tan x = sin x/cos x is undefined where cos x = 0
Near these lines the graph shoots to ±∞
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the asymptotes of tan and cot

teach.ask: Gappu is sketching y = sin x and y = tan x. Explain where each increases or decreases, and what the graphs look like.
teach.praise: A smooth wave for sin, a ladder of rising curves with walls for tan. Picture perfect!
teach.nudge: What happens to the graph of tan x near x = π/2?

revise.summary: sin and cos graphs are waves between −1 and 1 with period 2π, and cos is sin shifted left by π/2. tan increases in every quadrant with asymptotes at odd multiples of π/2; sec and cosec never enter −1 < y < 1.
focus: Describe how sin, cos and tan increase or decrease in each quadrant
Find zeros, maxima and asymptotes from the graphs
Relate the sin and cos graphs by a shift of π/2
remember: sin x: increases 0 → 1 in I, decreases 1 → 0 in II, 0 → −1 in III, increases −1 → 0 in IV
cos x: decreases 1 → 0 in I and 0 → −1 in II; increases −1 → 0 in III and 0 → 1 in IV
tan x increases in every quadrant; asymptotes at x = (2n + 1)π/2
cos x = sin(x + π/2): the sin graph shifted left by π/2
traps: sin x is zero at multiples of π, not at odd multiples of π/2
Don't forget both end points: sin x cuts the x-axis at 0, π and 2π on [0, 2π]

learn.hook: Every allied-angle trick — cos(π − x), sin(π/2 + x) — comes out of ONE formula: cos(x + y). Learn it once, and the rest follow.
points: cos(x + y) = cos x cos y − sin x sin y. It is proved from the unit circle by equating the distance between two pairs of points on it.
Replace y by −y: cos(x − y) = cos x cos y + sin x sin y.
cos(π/2 − x) = sin x, sin(π/2 − x) = cos x; cos(π/2 + x) = −sin x, sin(π/2 + x) = cos x.
cos(π − x) = −cos x, sin(π − x) = sin x; cos(π + x) = −cos x, sin(π + x) = −sin x.
cos(2π − x) = cos x, sin(2π − x) = −sin x.

example.q: Find cos 15° using cos(x − y).

learn.reallife: Phase-shift tricks such as cos(π/2 − x) = sin x are used in electrical engineering to compare AC voltages that are out of step.

games.title: Derive cos(x − y) from cos(x + y)
items: Start with cos(x + y) = cos x cos y − sin x sin y.
Use cos(−y) = cos y and sin(−y) = −sin y.
cos(x − y) = cos x cos y + sin x sin y.

quiz.q: cos(x + y) equals:
options: cos x cos y + sin x sin y

topics.title: The imaginary unit i and complex numbers

learn.hook: No real number squared gives −1. So mathematicians invented one: i. Today electrical engineers at power grids use it every day.
points: x² + 1 = 0 has no real solution, because x² ≥ 0 for every real x. We extend R by a new number i with i² = −1.
A complex number is z = a + ib with a, b real. Re z = a is the real part and Im z = b is the imaginary part. The set of complex numbers is C.
If b = 0, z = a is purely real; if a = 0 and b ≠ 0, z = ib is purely imaginary. So every real number is a complex number.
Equality: a + ib = c + id exactly when a = c AND b = d.
Note: Im z is the real number b, not ib. For z = 3 − 5i, Im z = −5.

learn.hook: Adding complex numbers is like adding bank balances in two separate accounts — real with real, imaginary with imaginary.
points: (a + ib) + (c + id) = (a + c) + i(b + d).
Properties of addition: closure, commutative z₁ + z₂ = z₂ + z₁, associative, additive identity 0 = 0 + 0i, additive inverse −z = −a − ib.
Subtraction: z₁ − z₂ = z₁ + (−z₂) = (a − c) + i(b − d).
Always simplify the final answer to the standard form a + ib.
Be careful with brackets: −(3 − 2i) = −3 + 2i.

topics.title: Powers of i and roots of negative numbers

learn.hook: i, −1, −i, 1, i, −1, … The powers of i repeat every four steps — like the four seasons, or the four innings of a Test match.
points: i¹ = i, i² = −1, i³ = −i, i⁴ = 1, and then the pattern repeats.
For any integer k: i^(4k) = 1, i^(4k+1) = i, i^(4k+2) = −1, i^(4k+3) = −i. Divide the power by 4 and use the remainder.
Negative powers: 1/i = −i, so i^(−n) = 1/iⁿ. For example i^(−3) = 1/(−i) = i.
Square root of a negative real: √(−a) = i√a for a > 0, e.g. √(−9) = 3i.
√a·√b = √(ab) is FALSE when both a and b are negative: √(−4)·√(−9) = (2i)(3i) = −6, not √36 = 6.

topics.title: Reciprocal and division of complex numbers

learn.hook: Dividing by 3 + 4i looks scary — until you multiply top and bottom by 3 − 4i and the i disappears from the denominator.
points: For z = a + ib ≠ 0, z·z̄ = (a + ib)(a − ib) = a² + b² = |z|², a real number.
Multiplicative inverse: z⁻¹ = 1/z = z̄/|z|² = (a − ib)/(a² + b²).
Division: z₁/z₂ = z₁ · (1/z₂) = z₁z̄₂/|z₂|², for z₂ ≠ 0.
In practice: multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator.
Check: z · z⁻¹ should equal 1.

learn.hook: The modulus of a complex number is its 'size' — the straight-line distance from the origin, just like how far a drone is from its launch pad.
points: For z = a + ib: modulus |z| = √(a² + b²) and conjugate z̄ = a − ib.
|z₁z₂| = |z₁||z₂| and |z₁/z₂| = |z₁|/|z₂| (z₂ ≠ 0).
Conjugates: (z₁ + z₂)‾ = z̄₁ + z̄₂, (z₁ − z₂)‾ = z̄₁ − z̄₂, (z₁z₂)‾ = z̄₁z̄₂, (z₁/z₂)‾ = z̄₁/z̄₂.
|z̄| = |z| and z + z̄ = 2 Re z, z − z̄ = 2i Im z.
Shortcut: to find the modulus of a product or quotient, find each modulus separately — no need to multiply out.
learn.reallife: GPS apps calculate the straight-line distance between two places with the same √(a² + b²) idea that gives the modulus.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

learn.hook: Complex numbers live on a map! Real part across, imaginary part up — and suddenly modulus is distance and conjugate is a mirror.
points: z = x + iy is plotted as the point (x, y). This plane is the complex plane or Argand plane.
The x-axis is the real axis (points a + 0i) and the y-axis is the imaginary axis (points 0 + ib). E.g. 2 + 4i is (2, 4) and −3 + i is (−3, 1) in quadrant II.
|z| = √(x² + y²) is the distance of the point (x, y) from the origin.
The conjugate z̄ = x − iy is the point (x, −y): the reflection of z in the real axis.
Syllabus note: polar form, square roots of complex numbers and complex roots of quadratic equations are not part of the current CBSE exam syllabus for this chapter.

learn.hook: You have ₹200 for samosas at ₹15 each. You can't spend MORE than you have — and that 'not more than' is an inequality: 15x ≤ 200.
points: Real life is full of limits: a budget, a speed limit, a minimum attendance. These are written as inequalities.
Two expressions compared with <, >, ≤ or ≥ form an inequality. 3 < 5 is numerical; x < 5 or 2x + 3y ≥ 6 is literal (it has variables).
Strict inequalities use < or >; slack (non-strict) ones use ≤ or ≥.
ax + b < 0 (a ≠ 0) is a linear inequality in one variable; ax + by ≥ c is linear in two variables; ax² + bx + c > 0 (a ≠ 0) is quadratic, not linear.
Turning words into symbols: 'at least' → ≥, 'at most / cannot exceed / not more than' → ≤, 'more than' → >, 'less than' → <.

quiz.mistake: Excludes the boundary value 75

teach.ask: Gappu doesn't know when to use < and when to use ≤. Explain strict and slack inequalities and how to turn words like 'at least' into symbols.
teach.praise: 'At least' is ≥, 'at most' is ≤, and strict means no equality. Got it!
teach.nudge: Does 'at least 18' include 18 itself? Which sign shows that?

revise.summary: An inequality compares two expressions with <, >, ≤ or ≥. Strict ones use < or >, slack ones use ≤ or ≥, and word limits like 'at least' and 'at most' become ≥ and ≤.
focus: Tell strict from slack inequalities, and numerical from literal ones
Classify inequalities as linear in one or two variables, or quadratic
Translate word conditions ('at least', 'at most', 'more than') into symbols
remember: Strict: < or >; slack (non-strict): ≤ or ≥
ax + b < 0 (a ≠ 0): linear in one variable; ax + by ≥ c: linear in two variables; ax² + bx + c > 0 (a ≠ 0): quadratic
'At least' → ≥; 'at most / cannot exceed / not more than' → ≤; 'more than' → >; 'less than' → <
traps: 'At most' includes equality: use ≤, not <
An inequality with x² or a product like xy is not linear

learn.hook: Solving an inequality is like solving an equation — with ONE trap: multiply or divide by a negative number and the sign flips.
points: A solution is a value that makes the inequality true; the set of all solutions is the solution set.
Rule 1: the same number may be added to (or subtracted from) both sides without changing the sign.
Rule 2: both sides may be multiplied or divided by the same POSITIVE number without changing the sign; for a NEGATIVE number, the sign reverses (< becomes >).
The answer depends on the allowed values: 30x < 200 gives x < 20/3, so x ∈ {1, 2, …, 6} if x ∈ N, x ∈ {…, 5, 6} if x ∈ Z, and all real x < 20/3 if x ∈ R.
With fractions, multiply through by the LCM of the denominators (a positive number) first; open brackets carefully.

example.q: Solve x/4 > x/3 + 1 for real x.
steps: Multiply by −1 and reverse the sign: x < −12.

learn.reallife: A Delhi metro card has ₹480. Each trip costs ₹40 and at least ₹100 must stay on the card: 480 − 40n ≥ 100 gives n ≤ 9.5, so at most 9 trips.

revise.summary: Solve a linear inequality like an equation, but if you multiply or divide both sides by a negative number, reverse the sign. The final solution set depends on whether x is natural, integer or real.

Don't include numbers that are not allowed, like 0 or negatives, when x ∈ N

topics.title: Number line, intervals, systems and double inequalities

learn.hook: A medicine is safe between 2 °C and 8 °C — not one, but two conditions at once. Systems and double inequalities handle exactly that.
points: On the number line, a filled (dark) circle means the end point is included (≤, ≥); a hollow circle means it is excluded (<, >).
Write answers in interval notation: x ≥ 2 → [2, ∞); x < −1 → (−∞, −1); −3 < x ≤ 5 → (−3, 5].
A system of inequalities: solve each one, then take the common part (intersection) of the solution sets.
A double inequality like a ≤ (px + q)/r ≤ b: do the same operation to all three parts; if you multiply or divide by a negative number, reverse BOTH signs.

example.q: Solve the system 2x + 1 > x − 3 and 3x − 2 ≤ 7, and write the answer as an interval.

learn.reallife: Vaccines in India's cold chain must stay between 2 °C and 8 °C: the double inequality 2 ≤ T ≤ 8, drawn as a closed segment on a thermometer.

revise.summary: Show solutions on the number line with filled circles for ≤, ≥ and hollow circles for <, >, and write them as intervals. For a system, take the common part; for a double inequality, do each step to all three parts.

Write solutions in interval notation
Solve systems of inequalities by intersecting the solution sets

System: solve each inequality, then take the intersection
Double inequality: apply each operation to all three parts

topics.title: Word problems: marks, integers and lengths

learn.hook: 'How much do I need in the last test to get 70% overall?' — the question every Class 11 student asks. Inequalities answer it.
points: Step 1: name the unknown. Step 2: translate the condition into an inequality. Step 3: solve. Step 4: keep only answers that make sense (whole numbers, positive lengths, etc.).
Average condition: (sum of scores)/(number of tests) ≥ target.
Consecutive odd (or even) integers: x and x + 2. Consecutive integers: x and x + 1.
Lengths: express every side or piece in terms of one variable; perimeter or total length gives the inequality.
Temperature: C = (5/9)(F − 32). A range in °F converts to a range in °C by applying the formula to both ends.

example.q: Aman scored 68 and 75 in the first two unit tests. What is the minimum he must score in the third test to have an average of at least 72?

learn.hook: 3 kurtas and 4 pairs of jeans: how many outfits? You don't need to list them — 3 × 4 = 12. That multiplication is the most powerful idea in counting.
points: Counting by listing is slow and error-prone; the counting principles let us count arrangements and selections without listing.
Multiplication principle: if one event can happen in m ways and, after it, another can happen in n ways, the two together can happen in m × n ways.
It extends to any number of events: m × n × p × … ways.
Use it for building codes, numbers, number plates and signals position by position: fill each place in turn and multiply the choices.
Example: signals made by hoisting 2 of 4 different flags one below the other: 4 × 3 = 12 signals.

example.q: How many 3-digit numbers can be formed from the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 if no digit is repeated?

learn.hook: Swap the two Os in 'BALLOON' and nothing changes. That's why arrangements of alike letters need dividing, not just multiplying.
points: If p of n objects are alike (and the rest different), the number of arrangements of all n is n!/p!.
Reason: swapping the p alike objects among themselves (p! ways) gives the same arrangement, so n! counts each one p! times.
If p₁, p₂, …, pₖ objects are alike of k kinds, the number of arrangements is n!/(p₁! p₂! … pₖ!).
Example: MISSISSIPPI has 11 letters with I × 4, S × 4, P × 2: 11!/(4! 4! 2!) = 34,650.
ALLAHABAD has 9 letters with A × 4, L × 2: 9!/(4! 2!) = 7560.

To find n from a relation like nP5 = 20 nP3, write both sides as products and cancel: (n − 3)(n − 4) = 20, so n = 8.

learn.hook: Choosing 3 friends for a trip to Goa is a combination — the order you pick them doesn't matter. Ranking them 1st, 2nd, 3rd would be a permutation.
points: A combination is a selection where order does not matter.
nCr = n!/(r!(n − r)!), 0 ≤ r ≤ n. Each selection of r objects can be arranged in r! ways, so nPr = r! × nCr.

If nCa = nCb, then a = b or a + b = n.
Pascal's rule: nCr + nC(r − 1) = (n + 1)Cr.

topics.title: Patterns in powers and Pascal's triangle

learn.hook: Can you find 98⁵ without multiplying 98 by itself five times? A triangle of numbers known in India as Meru Prastaara, centuries before Pascal, makes it easy.
points: Repeated multiplication of big powers like (98)⁵ or (a + b)ⁿ is slow; we want a formula.
(a + b)⁰ = 1, (a + b)¹ = a + b, (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b², (a + b)³ = a³ + 3a²b + 3ab² + b³, (a + b)⁴ = a⁴ + 4a³b + 6a²b² + 4ab³ + b⁴.
The coefficients form Pascal's triangle: each row starts and ends with 1, and every inner entry is the sum of the two entries just above it.
The entries of row n are ⁿC₀, ⁿC₁, …, ⁿCₙ — Pascal's rule ⁿCᵣ + ⁿCᵣ₋₁ = ⁿ⁺¹Cᵣ is exactly 'add the two above'.

example.q: Use Pascal's triangle to expand (a + b)⁵.
steps: Powers of a fall 5 → 0; powers of b rise 0 → 5.

learn.reallife: Counting Sanskrit verse metres in Pingala's Chhandaḥśāstra led to this pattern; the commentator Halayudha (10th century CE) described it as Meru Prastaara, long before Pascal.

learn.hook: One formula expands (a + b)ⁿ for every positive integer n — no matter how big. That's the binomial theorem.
points: (a + b)ⁿ = ⁿC₀ aⁿ + ⁿC₁ aⁿ⁻¹ b + ⁿC₂ aⁿ⁻² b² + … + ⁿCₙ bⁿ, for any positive integer n.
Why: (a + b)ⁿ is n brackets multiplied. A term aⁿ⁻ʳ bʳ appears once for every way of choosing b from r of the n brackets — ⁿCᵣ ways.
There are n + 1 terms. Powers of a fall from n to 0, powers of b rise from 0 to n, and in each term the indices add up to n.
The numbers ⁿCᵣ are the binomial coefficients; they read the same from both ends because ⁿCᵣ = ⁿCₙ₋ᵣ.
Syllabus note: the general-term and middle-term formulas are not part of the current CBSE syllabus for this chapter.

learn.hook: Put a minus sign in (x − y)ⁿ and the signs start alternating: + − + − … Spot that and expansions become automatic.
points: (x − y)ⁿ = ⁿC₀xⁿ − ⁿC₁xⁿ⁻¹y + ⁿC₂xⁿ⁻²y² − … + (−1)ⁿ ⁿCₙ yⁿ: signs alternate.
(1 + x)ⁿ = ⁿC₀ + ⁿC₁x + ⁿC₂x² + … + ⁿCₙxⁿ and (1 − x)ⁿ = ⁿC₀ − ⁿC₁x + ⁿC₂x² − … + (−1)ⁿ ⁿCₙxⁿ.
Put x = 1 in (1 + x)ⁿ: ⁿC₀ + ⁿC₁ + … + ⁿCₙ = 2ⁿ. The sum of the coefficients of any expansion = its value at x = 1.
For terms like (x² + 3/x)⁴, write a = x², b = 3/x and simplify powers carefully: (3/x)² = 9/x².

topics.title: Using the theorem: big powers, comparisons, divisibility

learn.hook: 96³ in your head? Write it as (100 − 4)³ and the binomial theorem does it in four easy terms.
points: Write the base near a round number: 96 = 100 − 4, 101 = 100 + 1, 0.98 = 1 − 0.02.
Comparisons: (1.01)¹⁰⁰⁰⁰⁰⁰ = (1 + 0.01)¹⁰⁰⁰⁰⁰⁰ = 1 + 1000000 × 0.01 + (positive terms) > 1 + 10000 > 10000.
Divisibility: write the base as 1 + k. Then (1 + k)ⁿ = 1 + nk + k²(…), so (1 + k)ⁿ − nk − 1 is a multiple of k².
Example: 6ⁿ = (1 + 5)ⁿ = 1 + 5n + 25(…), so 6ⁿ − 5n leaves remainder 1 on division by 25.

learn.hook: (√2 + 1)⁴ + (√2 − 1)⁴ looks messy — but add the two expansions and half the terms vanish, leaving a whole number.
points: (a + b)ⁿ + (a − b)ⁿ = 2[terms with even powers of b]; (a + b)ⁿ − (a − b)ⁿ = 2[terms with odd powers of b].
To find n and a from given terms: compare coefficients, e.g. if (1 + ax)ⁿ = 1 + 8x + 24x² + …, then na = 8 and ⁿC₂ a² = 24.
Trinomials: group two terms as one, e.g. (1 + x + x²)² = ((1 + x) + x²)², then expand twice.
Always simplify surds at the end: (√2)⁴ = 4, (√3)³ = 3√3.

learn.hook: India's population year by year, your SIP balance month by month, a phone's value after each year of use — all are sequences.
points: A sequence is an ordered list of numbers a₁, a₂, a₃, …; aₙ is the nth term or general term.
A finite sequence has a last term (e.g. the marks in 5 unit tests); an infinite sequence goes on forever (e.g. 1, 1/2, 1/3, …).
Formally, a sequence is a function whose domain is N (or {1, 2, …, k} for a finite one): n ↦ aₙ.
Some sequences are given by a recurrence: earlier terms define later ones.
Fibonacci sequence: a₁ = a₂ = 1, aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + aₙ₋₂ for n > 2: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, …

learn.reallife: The Fibonacci numbers show up in sunflower seed spirals and pine cones — and in the counting of Sanskrit metres studied by Virahanka and Hemachandra long before Fibonacci.

learn.hook: One bacterium becomes 2, then 4, then 8 … In a GP each term is the previous one multiplied by the same number — and the numbers explode.
points: A G.P. is a sequence in which each term (after the first) is a fixed non-zero multiple of the previous one: aₖ₊₁/aₖ = r, the common ratio.

Three numbers in G.P. are best taken as a/r, a, ar (product a³); four as a/r³, a/r, ar, ar³.
If r > 1 (and a > 0) the terms grow; if 0 < r < 1 they shrink; if r < 0 the signs alternate.

topics.title: G.P. in real life and G.P. proofs

learn.hook: Bacteria in a lab, money in a fixed deposit, the value of a used scooter — they all multiply by the same factor each period.
points: Growth: P, Pk, Pk², … with k > 1 (e.g. bacteria tripling: k = 3).
Compound interest: ₹P at r% per year becomes P(1 + r/100)ⁿ after n years — the (n + 1)th term of a G.P.
Depreciation at r% per year: value after n years = P(1 − r/100)ⁿ.
Ancestors: 2 parents, 4 grandparents, 8 great-grandparents, … (assuming no common ancestors).
Proof idea: to show x, y, z are in G.P., show y² = xz (or y/x = z/y). E.g. if a, b, c are in G.P. then b² = ac, so (b²)² = a²c², and a², b², c² are in G.P.

example.q: A culture starts with 50 bacteria, and the number triples every hour. How many are there after 4 hours?

learn.reallife: A car bought for ₹8,00,000 that loses 20% of its value each year is worth 8,00,000 × (0.8)³ = ₹4,09,600 after 3 years — used-car dealers apply this formula every day.

learn.hook: For any two positive numbers, the arithmetic mean is never smaller than the geometric mean. This tiny fact solves optimisation puzzles from fencing to packaging.
points: For positive a and b: A = (a + b)/2 and G = √(ab).
Proof: A − G = (a + b)/2 − √(ab) = (√a − √b)²/2 ≥ 0. So A ≥ G, with equality exactly when a = b.
Given A and G, the numbers are the roots of x² − 2Ax + G² = 0, i.e. A ± √(A² − G²).
Ratio problems: if A : G is given, write a and b in terms of √a and √b, or use a + b = 2A and ab = G².
For a G.P. of n terms with sum S, product P and sum of reciprocals R: P²Rⁿ = Sⁿ.

A = G when the two numbers are equal.
If A = 13 and G = 12, the numbers are 18 and 8.
a + b = 26, ab = 144: roots of x² − 26x + 144 = 0 are 18 and 8.
A.M. ≥ G.M. holds for negative numbers too.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): For positive a and b, (a + b)/2 ≥ √(ab).
Reason (R): (√a − √b)² ≥ 0 for all positive a, b.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Expanding R gives a + b ≥ 2√(ab), which is A. So R explains A.
steps: R: (√a − √b)² ≥ 0, since a square is never negative: true
Expand: a − 2√(ab) + b ≥ 0 → a + b ≥ 2√(ab) → (a + b)/2 ≥ √(ab), which is A
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not connect the square with the inequality

teach.praise: A perfect square can't be negative, so A ≥ G. And the numbers come out of a quadratic. Convinced!
teach.nudge: Why is (√a − √b)² never negative, and what does that tell us?

revise.summary: For positive a and b, the A.M. (a + b)/2 is at least the G.M. √(ab), because A − G = (√a − √b)²/2 ≥ 0, with equality only when a = b. Given A and G, the numbers are the roots of x² − 2Ax + G² = 0.
focus: Prove A ≥ G using (√a − √b)² ≥ 0
Find two numbers from their A.M. and G.M.
Solve ratio problems and least-value problems with A.M. ≥ G.M.
remember: A − G = (√a − √b)²/2 ≥ 0, equality ⇔ a = b
Numbers with A.M. A and G.M. G are roots of x² − 2Ax + G² = 0: A ± √(A² − G²)
a + b = 2A and ab = G²
For a G.P.: P²Rⁿ = Sⁿ
traps: The product of the numbers is G², not G
A − G is (√a − √b)²/2, not (a − b)²/2

topics.title: Coordinate recall and slope of a line

learn.hook: Indian Railways signs say 'gradient 1 in 100' on the ghats — that is a slope. Coordinate geometry turns such steepness into a single number m.
points: Recall: distance PQ = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²); internal section point ((mx₂ + nx₁)/(m + n), (my₂ + ny₁)/(m + n)); triangle area = ½|x₁(y₂ − y₃) + x₂(y₃ − y₁) + x₃(y₁ − y₂)|.
Coordinate geometry links algebra and geometry: a line becomes an equation, and geometric facts become calculations.
The inclination θ of a line is the angle it makes with the positive x-axis, measured anticlockwise, 0° ≤ θ < 180°.
Slope m = tan θ (θ ≠ 90°). A horizontal line has m = 0; the slope of a vertical line is not defined.
Through (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂), x₁ ≠ x₂: m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁).

example.q: Find the slope of the line through (3, −2) and (−1, 4), and say whether its inclination is acute or obtuse.
steps: A negative slope means tan θ < 0, so 90° < θ < 180°.

learn.reallife: A railway gradient board reading '1 in 100' means the track rises 1 m for every 100 m — a slope of 1/100.

quiz.q: What is the slope of a line inclined at 30° to the positive x-axis?
quiz.mistake: Uses sin 30° instead of tan 30°

quiz.q: Find the slope of the line through (−2, 3) and (4, −6).
quiz.mistake: Puts the x-difference on top

quiz.q: A line has slope −1. What is its inclination?
quiz.explain: tan θ = −1 with 0° ≤ θ < 180° gives θ = 135°.
quiz.mistake: Gives a negative angle or one outside [0°, 180°)

quiz.q: The slope of the line through (5, 1) and (5, 7) is:
quiz.explain: x₂ − x₁ = 0, so the line is vertical and its slope is not defined.
steps: Both points have x = 5, so the line is vertical
quiz.mistake: Thinks a vertical line has slope 0

quiz.q: The distance between (2, −1) and (−4, 7) is:
quiz.mistake: Adds the differences instead of squaring

quiz.q: The point dividing the segment from (1, 2) to (7, 8) internally in the ratio 1 : 2 is:
quiz.mistake: Swaps m and n and gets (5, 6)

quiz.q: Using slopes, are A(1, 1), B(2, 3), C(4, 7) collinear?
options: Yes, because they have positive coordinates
quiz.explain: Slope AB = (3 − 1)/(2 − 1) = 2 and slope BC = (7 − 3)/(4 − 2) = 2; equal slopes through a common point B means collinear.
steps: Equal slopes and a common point B → same line
Answer: Yes, slope AB = slope BC = 2
quiz.mistake: Compares coordinates instead of slopes

quiz.q: If the line through (k, 3) and (2, 7) has slope 2, then k is:
quiz.mistake: Solves 4/(2 − k) = 2 as k = 4

teach.ask: Gappu thinks a vertical cliff has slope 0 because 'it doesn't go anywhere sideways'. Explain inclination and slope.
teach.praise: Slope is rise over run, tan θ — and a vertical line has no defined slope. Cliff confusion over!
teach.nudge: What is the 'run' for a vertical line, and what goes wrong when you divide by it?

revise.summary: The inclination θ of a line is its angle with the positive x-axis (0° ≤ θ < 180°), and its slope is m = tan θ = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). Horizontal lines have slope 0; vertical lines have no defined slope.
focus: Find slope from an inclination or from two points
Find the inclination from a slope, including obtuse angles
Use distance, section and slope formulas from coordinate geometry
Check collinearity with equal slopes
remember: m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁), x₁ ≠ x₂
Distance PQ = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²)
Section point (internal, m : n) = ((mx₂ + nx₁)/(m + n), (my₂ + ny₁)/(m + n))
traps: A vertical line's slope is not defined; it is not 0
Inclination is measured from 0° to 180°, so slope −1 means 135°, not −45°

learn.hook: Railway tracks never meet: equal slopes. A road crossing them at a level crossing makes a right angle: slopes multiply to −1.
points: Two non-vertical lines are parallel exactly when their slopes are equal: m₁ = m₂.
Two non-vertical lines are perpendicular exactly when m₁m₂ = −1 (slopes are negative reciprocals).
A horizontal line (m = 0) is perpendicular to every vertical line.
Three points A, B, C are collinear exactly when slope AB = slope BC.
A linear relation between two quantities (cost and units, °C and °F) has a straight-line graph; its slope is the rate of change.

example.q: Using slopes, show that A(0, 0), B(2, 2), C(3, −3) form a right triangle.

learn.reallife: Hostel fees: ₹50,000 for 0 extra months and ₹62,000 for 3 extra months fit the line F = 4000m + 50,000; the slope ₹4000 per month is the rate of change.

games.title: Slope relationships
items: Lines with slopes 3 and −1/3 are perpendicular.
Lines with slopes 2 and −2 are perpendicular.
If slope AB = slope BC, then A, B, C are collinear.
Same slope and a common point B means the same line.
Two lines with slopes 0 and 0 can be perpendicular.
Both are horizontal, so they are parallel.

quiz.q: A line is perpendicular to a line of slope 3/4. What is its slope?
quiz.mistake: Takes the reciprocal but forgets the minus sign

quiz.q: The line through (−1, 2) and (2, 8) is perpendicular to the line through (4, 5) and (x, 1). Find x.
quiz.explain: First slope = 6/3 = 2, so the second slope must be −1/2: (1 − 5)/(x − 4) = −1/2 ⇒ x − 4 = 8 ⇒ x = 12.
quiz.mistake: Sets the slopes equal (parallel) instead

quiz.q: If A(0, 0), B(4, 1), C(6, 4), D(2, 3) are joined in order, which pairs of sides are parallel?
quiz.explain: Slope AB = 1/4 = slope DC; slope BC = 3/2 = slope AD. So ABCD is a parallelogram.
steps: Answer: AB ∥ DC and BC ∥ AD
quiz.mistake: Compares adjacent sides instead of opposite ones

quiz.q: For what k are the points (1, 2), (3, 6) and (k, 10) collinear?
steps: For collinearity, slope from (3, 6) to (k, 10) must be 2
quiz.mistake: Uses the wrong pair of points

quiz.q: A taxi charges ₹100 for 5 km and ₹180 for 15 km, following a straight line. What is the charge per km (the slope)?
quiz.mistake: Divides 180 by 15

quiz.q: In the taxi example above, what is the fixed charge (the value at 0 km)?
quiz.explain: C = 8d + c with 100 = 40 + c, so c = 60.
quiz.mistake: Takes the 5 km charge as the fixed charge

quiz.q: Lines with slopes m and −1/m (m ≠ 0) are:
steps: Product −1 is the condition for perpendicular lines
quiz.mistake: Thinks negative slopes make lines parallel

quiz.q: Which pair of lines is parallel?
quiz.explain: 4x − 2y = 7 gives y = 2x − 7/2, slope 2, same as y = 2x + 3.
quiz.mistake: Compares the constants instead of the slopes

teach.ask: Gappu wants to check if two roads are parallel or meet at right angles using only slopes. Explain the conditions.
teach.praise: Equal slopes — parallel; product −1 — perpendicular. Road planning sorted!
teach.nudge: What must the product of the slopes be for perpendicular lines?

revise.summary: Non-vertical lines are parallel when their slopes are equal and perpendicular when the product of their slopes is −1. Three points are collinear when slope AB = slope BC, and a linear relation's slope is its rate of change.
focus: Use m₁ = m₂ for parallel and m₁m₂ = −1 for perpendicular lines
Find an unknown coordinate from a parallel or perpendicular condition
Test collinearity and classify quadrilaterals with slopes
Interpret slope and intercept in real linear relations
remember: Parallel: m₁ = m₂
Perpendicular: m₁m₂ = −1 (slopes are negative reciprocals)
A, B, C collinear ⇔ slope AB = slope BC
Linear relation: slope = rate of change
traps: Perpendicular slopes are negative reciprocals: 3/4 → −4/3, not −3/4
Rewrite an equation in y = mx + c form before reading its slope

learn.hook: Two runways at an airport cross at an angle; air-traffic engineers compute it straight from the slopes.
points: If lines have slopes m₁ and m₂ (1 + m₁m₂ ≠ 0), the acute angle θ between them satisfies tan θ = |(m₂ − m₁)/(1 + m₁m₂)|.
The obtuse angle between them is 180° − θ.
If 1 + m₁m₂ = 0, the lines are perpendicular (θ = 90°).
To find an unknown slope from the angle, remove the modulus: (m₂ − m₁)/(1 + m₁m₂) = ± tan θ, giving two answers.

example.q: The angle between two lines is π/4 and one slope is 1/3. Find the other slope.

learn.reallife: Crossing runways at an airport such as Mumbai's are set at an angle to suit the wind; the angle comes straight from their slopes.

games.title: Find the acute angle between slopes 2 and −3

quiz.q: Find the acute angle between lines with slopes √3 and 1/√3.
quiz.explain: These lines are inclined at 60° and 30°, so the angle between them is 30°. (tan θ = |(√3 − 1/√3)/(1 + 1)| = 1/√3.)
quiz.mistake: Adds the inclinations

quiz.q: For lines with slopes m₁ and m₂, the lines are perpendicular when:
quiz.explain: Then the formula's denominator is 0, tan θ is undefined and θ = 90°.
steps: When 1 + m₁m₂ = 0 the denominator is 0 and tan θ is undefined
quiz.mistake: Uses m₁ + m₂ = 0

quiz.q: What is tan θ for the acute angle between y = 2x + 1 and y = 3x − 4?
quiz.mistake: Forgets the 1 in the denominator

quiz.q: The acute angle between two lines is 45° and one slope is 2. Which pair gives all possible values of the other slope?
quiz.mistake: Drops the modulus and keeps only one case

quiz.q: The obtuse angle between two lines whose acute angle is 50° is:
quiz.explain: The angles between two crossing lines are θ and 180° − θ.
steps: Two crossing lines make angles θ and 180° − θ
quiz.mistake: Subtracts from 90° or 360°

quiz.q: Find the acute angle between the x-axis and the line through (0, 0) and (1, √3).
quiz.explain: Slope √3 = tan 60°, and the x-axis has slope 0.
quiz.mistake: Uses cot instead of tan

quiz.q: Lines have slopes 3 and −1/2. tan of the acute angle between them is:
steps: tan θ = |(m₂ − m₁)/(1 + m₁m₂)| with m₁ = 3, m₂ = −1/2
quiz.mistake: Gets the reciprocal by swapping numerator and denominator

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The formula tan θ = |(m₂ − m₁)/(1 + m₁m₂)| gives the acute angle between two lines.
Reason (R): The modulus makes tan θ non-negative.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A non-negative tangent corresponds to an angle in [0°, 90°), i.e. the acute (or zero) angle; that is why the modulus is used.
steps: R: a modulus is never negative, so tan θ ≥ 0 — true
tan θ ≥ 0 means 0° ≤ θ < 90°, the acute angle — so A is true
The modulus in R is the reason A gives the acute angle
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not link the modulus to choosing the acute angle

teach.ask: Gappu needs the angle between two lines with slopes 1/2 and 3. Explain the formula and why it has a modulus sign.
teach.praise: Difference over one-plus-product, with a modulus for the acute angle. 45° it is!
teach.nudge: What does the modulus do to the value of tan θ?

revise.summary: The acute angle θ between lines with slopes m₁ and m₂ satisfies tan θ = |(m₂ − m₁)/(1 + m₁m₂)|; the obtuse angle is 180° − θ. If 1 + m₁m₂ = 0 the lines are perpendicular.
focus: Find the acute angle between two lines from their slopes
Find the obtuse angle as 180° − θ
Find an unknown slope from the angle, using ± to get both answers
remember: tan θ = |(m₂ − m₁)/(1 + m₁m₂)|, 1 + m₁m₂ ≠ 0
Obtuse angle = 180° − θ
1 + m₁m₂ = 0 → lines are perpendicular
traps: When finding an unknown slope, remove the modulus with ± and keep both answers
Don't drop the modulus when you want the acute angle

learn.hook: Give a GPS one point and a direction, or two points, and it can draw your road. Those are the point-slope and two-point forms.
points: Horizontal line through (a, b): y = b. Vertical line through (a, b): x = a. The x-axis is y = 0 and the y-axis is x = 0.
Point-slope form: the line through (x₀, y₀) with slope m is y − y₀ = m(x − x₀).
Two-point form: through (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂): y − y₁ = [(y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁)](x − x₁).
A point lies on a line exactly when its coordinates satisfy the equation.
Simplify to the form Ax + By + C = 0 for the final answer.

example.q: Find the equation of the line through (−2, 3) with slope −4.

learn.reallife: Delhi Metro planners describe a straight track segment between two stations by the two-point form using the stations' map coordinates.

quiz.q: The equation of the line through (3, −2) with slope 2 is:
quiz.mistake: Uses y − 2 instead of y + 2

quiz.q: The line through (1, 2) and (−3, 4) is:
quiz.mistake: Gets the slope sign wrong

quiz.q: Which is the equation of the vertical line through (−4, 7)?
quiz.explain: Every point on a vertical line has the same x-coordinate.
steps: A vertical line has the same x-coordinate at every point
quiz.mistake: Confuses vertical and horizontal

quiz.q: Does the point (2, 1) lie on 3x − 4y − 2 = 0?
quiz.explain: Substituting gives 0, so the point satisfies the equation.
quiz.mistake: Makes an arithmetic slip when substituting

quiz.q: The line through (0, 0) and (−2, 6) is:
quiz.mistake: Drops the negative sign of the slope

quiz.q: A line passes through (2, 3) and has inclination 45°. Its equation is:
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the sign when moving terms

quiz.q: For what value of k does the line through (1, k) and (3, 7) also pass through (5, 11)?
steps: Slope from (1, k) to (3, 7) must also be 2: (7 − k)/2 = 2
quiz.mistake: Uses the slope 4 between y-values

quiz.q: The y-coordinate of the point on the line through (1, 1) and (4, 7) with x = 3 is:
quiz.mistake: Uses slope 3

teach.ask: Gappu knows one point on a road and its slope. Explain how to write the road's equation, and how to do it with two points instead.
teach.praise: One point plus slope, or two points — find the slope and plug in. Roads drawn!
teach.nudge: If you have two points, what do you calculate first?

revise.summary: A line through (x₀, y₀) with slope m is y − y₀ = m(x − x₀); through two points, first find the slope and then use point-slope form. Horizontal lines are y = b and vertical lines are x = a.
focus: Write lines in point-slope and two-point forms
Write horizontal and vertical lines through a point
Check whether a point lies on a line by substitution
Simplify the final answer to Ax + By + C = 0
remember: Horizontal line through (a, b): y = b; vertical line: x = a
Point-slope: y − y₀ = m(x − x₀)
Two-point: y − y₁ = [(y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁)](x − x₁)
A point lies on a line ⇔ its coordinates satisfy the equation
traps: A vertical line through (−4, 7) is x = −4, not y = −4
Watch signs when substituting: y − (−2) = y + 2

learn.hook: Your phone bill = fixed rental + rate × minutes: y = mx + c. The fixed part is the intercept, the rate is the slope.
points: Slope-intercept form: y = mx + c, where c is the y-intercept (the line meets the y-axis at (0, c)).
With x-intercept d: y = m(x − d).
Intercept form: x/a + y/b = 1 meets the x-axis at (a, 0) and the y-axis at (0, b).
From Ax + By + C = 0 (B ≠ 0): slope = −A/B and y-intercept = −C/B; for C ≠ 0, x-intercept = −C/A and y-intercept = −C/B.
Real data: if price p and demand d are linearly related, two data points give the line, and it predicts other values.

example.q: Reduce 3x + 4y − 12 = 0 to slope-intercept and intercept forms.

learn.reallife: A Pune dairy sells 1000 L of milk a day at ₹40/L and 900 L at ₹45/L. Assuming a linear relation, it predicts sales of 800 L at ₹50/L.

items.text: x + 7y = 0 in slope form: y = ___ x

quiz.q: Find the slope and y-intercept of 6x + 3y − 5 = 0.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to divide the constant by 3

quiz.q: The line with x-intercept 3 and y-intercept −2 is:
steps: Check: y = 0 gives x = 3; x = 0 gives y = −2
quiz.mistake: Swaps the intercepts or drops the minus sign

quiz.q: The line through (−3, 5) that cuts off equal intercepts on the axes is:
quiz.explain: x/a + y/a = 1 ⇒ x + y = a. Substitute: −3 + 5 = 2 = a.
steps: Equal intercepts a: x/a + y/a = 1 → x + y = a
So the line is x + y = 2
quiz.mistake: Uses x − y for equal intercepts

quiz.q: What is the x-intercept of 3x − 4y + 12 = 0?
quiz.mistake: Puts x = 0 and finds the y-intercept

quiz.q: A dairy sells 1000 L of milk a day at ₹40/L and 900 L at ₹45/L. Assuming a linear relation, how much will it sell at ₹50/L?
quiz.mistake: Takes the change of 100 L per ₹1 instead of per ₹5

quiz.q: The line y = mx + c passes through (1, 4) and (3, 10). What is c?
quiz.mistake: Confuses c with m

quiz.q: Which equation has slope −3/2 and y-intercept 4?
steps: Bring all terms to one side
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the coefficients of x and y

quiz.q: A rod's length L (cm) depends linearly on temperature T (°C): L = 120.04 at 10 °C and 120.24 at 60 °C. By how many cm does it grow per °C?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to divide by the 50 °C change

teach.ask: Gappu's phone plan costs ₹199 fixed plus ₹1 per minute. Explain y = mx + c and the intercept form x/a + y/b = 1.
teach.praise: Slope is the rate, intercept is the fixed part, and x/a + y/b = 1 shows where the axes are cut. Bill decoded!
teach.nudge: In y = mx + c, which letter is the fixed starting value?

revise.summary: The slope-intercept form y = mx + c has slope m and y-intercept c, and the intercept form x/a + y/b = 1 cuts the axes at (a, 0) and (0, b). For Ax + By + C = 0, the slope is −A/B and the y-intercept is −C/B.
focus: Convert a general equation to slope-intercept and intercept forms
Find intercepts by putting x = 0 or y = 0
Write lines from given intercepts, including equal intercepts
Build a linear model from two data points and predict
remember: y = mx + c: slope m, y-intercept c
x/a + y/b = 1: intercepts a on the x-axis and b on the y-axis
Ax + By + C = 0: slope −A/B, y-intercept −C/B, x-intercept −C/A
traps: Keep the sign of a negative intercept: x/3 + y/(−2) = 1, not x/3 + y/2 = 1
The x-intercept comes from putting y = 0, not x = 0

topics.title: Lines in triangles; parallel and perpendicular lines through a point

learn.hook: Every triangle hides special lines — medians, altitudes, perpendicular bisectors. With slopes and midpoints you can write each one.
points: Median from A: the line through A and the midpoint of BC.
Altitude from A: through A, perpendicular to BC (slope = −1/slope of BC).
Perpendicular bisector of PQ: through the midpoint of PQ, perpendicular to PQ.
Line parallel to Ax + By + C = 0 through (x₁, y₁): Ax + By = Ax₁ + By₁ (same A, B).
Line perpendicular to Ax + By + C = 0 through (x₁, y₁): Bx − Ay = Bx₁ − Ay₁ (swap A, B and change one sign).

example.q: Find the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining (1, 2) and (5, 6).
steps: Slope of segment: (6 − 2)/(5 − 1) = 1, so perpendicular slope −1.

learn.reallife: Surveyors locating a new well equidistant from two villages use the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them.

games.title: Triangle line ↔ what it passes through
pairs: A and the midpoint of BC
Midpoint of BC, perpendicular to BC
Line parallel to BC through A

quiz.q: The line through (−2, 3) perpendicular to 3x − 4y + 2 = 0 is:
quiz.explain: Perpendicular: 4x + 3y + k = 0. Substitute: −8 + 9 + k = 0 ⇒ k = −1.
steps: Perpendicular to 3x − 4y + 2 = 0: swap A, B and change one sign → 4x + 3y + k = 0
quiz.mistake: Keeps the same coefficients (parallel line)

quiz.q: Triangle A(2, 1), B(4, 3), C(6, 1). The median from B passes through:
quiz.explain: The midpoint of AC is ((2 + 6)/2, (1 + 1)/2) = (4, 1).
steps: The median from B goes to the midpoint of AC
quiz.mistake: Takes the midpoint of AB or BC

quiz.q: In the same triangle, the median from B has equation:
quiz.explain: B(4, 3) and (4, 1) have the same x-coordinate, so the median is the vertical line x = 4.
steps: Median from B joins B(4, 3) to the midpoint (4, 1)
quiz.mistake: Tries to compute a slope and divides by zero

quiz.q: Triangle A(0, 0), B(4, 0), C(1, 3). The altitude from A is perpendicular to BC. Its equation is:
quiz.explain: Slope BC = (3 − 0)/(1 − 4) = −1, so the altitude has slope 1 and passes through the origin: y = x.
quiz.mistake: Uses the slope of BC itself

quiz.q: The perpendicular bisector of the segment from (3, 4) to (−1, 2) is:
quiz.explain: Midpoint (1, 3); segment slope (2 − 4)/(−1 − 3) = 1/2, so perpendicular slope −2: y − 3 = −2(x − 1) ⇒ 2x + y − 5 = 0.
steps: Slope of segment = (2 − 4)/(−1 − 3) = 1/2, so perpendicular slope = −2
quiz.mistake: Forgets to use the midpoint

quiz.q: Which line is parallel to 2x + 5y − 7 = 0 and passes through the origin?
quiz.explain: Same A and B for parallel lines; through (0, 0) the constant is 0.
steps: Parallel lines keep the same A and B: 2x + 5y + k = 0
quiz.mistake: Swaps coefficients, giving a perpendicular line

quiz.q: The line through (1, 2) perpendicular to the line x − 2y + 3 = 0 has slope:
quiz.explain: Slope of x − 2y + 3 = 0 is 1/2; perpendicular slope −2.
quiz.mistake: Takes the reciprocal without the minus sign

quiz.q: For what value of p is the line px + 4y − 7 = 0 parallel to 3x + 2y + 1 = 0?
steps: Slope of px + 4y − 7 = 0 is −p/4; slope of 3x + 2y + 1 = 0 is −3/2
quiz.mistake: Equates p with 3 directly

teach.ask: Gappu must find the altitude of a triangle from vertex A. Explain how to write altitudes, medians and lines parallel or perpendicular to a given line.
teach.praise: Medians use midpoints, altitudes use perpendicular slopes, and parallels keep the same slope. Triangle tools ready!
teach.nudge: For an altitude, how is its slope related to the slope of the opposite side?

revise.summary: Medians join a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side, altitudes are perpendicular to the opposite side, and perpendicular bisectors pass through a midpoint at right angles. Parallel lines keep A and B; perpendicular lines swap them and change one sign.
focus: Find equations of medians, altitudes and perpendicular bisectors
Write a line parallel to Ax + By + C = 0 through a point
Write a line perpendicular to Ax + By + C = 0 through a point
Find an unknown coefficient from a parallel condition
remember: Median from A: through A and the midpoint of BC
Altitude from A: through A with slope −1/(slope of BC)
Parallel to Ax + By + C = 0 through (x₁, y₁): Ax + By = Ax₁ + By₁
Perpendicular through (x₁, y₁): Bx − Ay = Bx₁ − Ay₁
traps: An altitude goes through the vertex, not through the midpoint of the opposite side
The slope of x − 2y + 3 = 0 is 1/2 (−A/B), not −1/2

topics.title: Distance of a point from a line

learn.hook: How far is your house from a straight highway? Not along any road — the shortest distance, straight across at a right angle. One formula gives it.
points: The perpendicular distance of (x₁, y₁) from Ax + By + C = 0 is d = |Ax₁ + By₁ + C|/√(A² + B²).
It is derived by finding the area of the triangle formed by P and the intercepts of the line in two ways (½ × base × height and by coordinates).
Distance between parallel lines Ax + By + C₁ = 0 and Ax + By + C₂ = 0: |C₁ − C₂|/√(A² + B²).
Make sure both parallel lines have the SAME A and B before using the formula (e.g. rewrite 6x + 8y + 10 = 0 as 3x + 4y + 5 = 0).
Points at a given distance from a line: set the distance formula equal to the value and solve with ±.

example.q: Find the distance of (2, 3) from 3x + 4y − 3 = 0.

teach.ask: Gappu wants the shortest distance from his nest to a straight power line 3x + 4y − 12 = 0. Explain the distance formula and how to use it for parallel lines.
must: root of a squared plus b squared

focus: Find the distance of a point from a line
Find the distance between two parallel lines after matching A and B
Find points or unknowns at a given distance from a line, using ±

Parallel lines: d = |C₁ − C₂|/√(A² + B²)
