topics.title: Feet, images, concurrency and mixed problems

learn.hook: A ray of light bounces off a mirror at the same angle it hits. Coordinate geometry finds exactly where — using images of points in lines.
points: Foot of the perpendicular from P to a line: the point on the line where the perpendicular through P meets it.
Image (reflection) of P in a line: the line is the perpendicular bisector of P and its image P′. The midpoint of PP′ lies on the line and PP′ is perpendicular to it.
Lines with equal intercepts: x + y = a. Through a point (x₁, y₁): a = x₁ + y₁.
Three lines are concurrent if the intersection of two of them lies on the third.
Reflection problems: the image of the source in the mirror line, joined to the target point, gives the reflected ray.

example.q: Find the image of (2, 1) in the line x + y − 5 = 0.
steps: Let the image be (h, k). PP′ is perpendicular to the line (slope −1), so PP′ has slope 1: (k − 1)/(h − 2) = 1 ⇒ k = h − 1.
Midpoint ((h + 2)/2, (k + 1)/2) lies on the line: (h + 2)/2 + (k + 1)/2 = 5 ⇒ h + k = 7.

learn.reallife: Snooker and carrom players aim at a cushion's 'image point' to bank a shot — the same reflection geometry.

games.title: Find k so that x + y = 3, 2x − y = 0 and kx + 3y = 8 are concurrent
Mixed line facts
items: The image of (3, 5) in the x-axis is (3, −5).
Reflection in y = 0 changes the sign of y.
The image of (1, 2) in the line y = x is (2, 1).
Reflection in y = x swaps the coordinates.
The foot of the perpendicular from (0, 0) to x + y = 2 is (2, 0).
It is (1, 1); (2, 0) is only the x-intercept.
The line through (2, 3) with equal intercepts is x + y = 5.
Three lines are concurrent if all three are parallel.
Parallel lines never meet; concurrent lines pass through one common point.

quiz.q: The foot of the perpendicular from (0, 0) to the line x + y = 4 is:
quiz.explain: The perpendicular from the origin is y = x; it meets x + y = 4 at (2, 2).
steps: The perpendicular from the origin to x + y = 4 has slope 1: y = x
Solve with x + y = 4: x + x = 4
quiz.mistake: Picks an intercept point

quiz.q: The image of (4, 1) in the line x + y = 0 is:
quiz.explain: Reflection in y = −x sends (a, b) to (−b, −a), so (4, 1) → (−1, −4).
steps: Reflection in y = −x sends (a, b) to (−b, −a)
quiz.mistake: Uses the rule for y = x

quiz.q: Find k so that the lines x + y = 3, 2x − y = 0 and kx + 3y = 8 are concurrent.
quiz.explain: The first two meet at (1, 2). Then k(1) + 3(2) = 8 ⇒ k = 2.
steps: Solve x + y = 3 and 2x − y = 0: add → 3x = 3, x = 1, y = 2
quiz.mistake: Substitutes into the wrong line

quiz.q: The equation of the line through (4, −1) making equal intercepts on the axes is:
quiz.explain: x + y = a with a = 4 + (−1) = 3.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts the coordinates

quiz.q: Find the foot of the perpendicular from (1, 3) to the line y = x.
quiz.explain: The perpendicular through (1, 3) has slope −1: y − 3 = −(x − 1), i.e. x + y = 4. It meets y = x at (2, 2).
steps: y = x has slope 1, so the perpendicular has slope −1
Meets y = x at x = 2, y = 2
quiz.mistake: Gives the image (3, 1) instead of the foot

quiz.q: If the foot of the perpendicular from P(1, 3) to a line is (2, 2), what is the image of P in that line?
quiz.explain: The foot is the midpoint of P and its image: image = 2(2, 2) − (1, 3) = (3, 1).
steps: The foot (2, 2) is the midpoint of P(1, 3) and its image P′
quiz.mistake: Confuses the foot with the image

quiz.q: A ray from (1, 2) is reflected by the x-axis and then passes through (5, 3). At which point does it meet the x-axis?
quiz.explain: Image of (1, 2) in the x-axis is (1, −2). The line through (1, −2) and (5, 3) has slope 5/4; it meets y = 0 at x = 1 + 2 × 4/5 = 13/5.
quiz.mistake: Joins (1, 2) directly to (5, 3)

quiz.q: Find the acute angle between the lines x − √3 y = 0 and √3 x − y = 0.
quiz.explain: Slopes 1/√3 and √3 (inclinations 30° and 60°), so the angle is 30°.
quiz.mistake: Adds the inclinations

teach.ask: Gappu wants to know where a light ray from a torch hits a mirror line before reaching his eye. Explain images of points and the foot of the perpendicular.
teach.praise: Reflect the source, join it to the target, and the mirror point appears. Light-bending maths!
teach.nudge: How are a point, its image and the foot of the perpendicular related?

revise.summary: The foot of the perpendicular from P is where the perpendicular through P meets the line, and the image P′ of P is such that the line is the perpendicular bisector of PP′. Three lines are concurrent if two meet at a point on the third.
focus: Find the foot of the perpendicular from a point to a line
Find the image (reflection) of a point in a line
Test or force concurrency of three lines
Write lines with equal intercepts through a point
remember: Foot: intersection of the line with the perpendicular through P
Image P′: foot = midpoint of PP′, so P′ = 2 × foot − P
Equal intercepts: x + y = a, with a = x₁ + y₁
Concurrent: the meeting point of two lines satisfies the third
traps: The foot is not the image: the image is twice as far from P
Reflection in y = −x sends (a, b) to (−b, −a), not (b, a)

learn.hook: Slice an ice-cream cone straight across: a circle. Tilt the knife: an ellipse. Tilt more: a parabola, then a hyperbola. Four curves, one cone.
points: Conic sections (conics) are the curves obtained when a plane cuts a double cone. They describe planetary orbits (ellipses), telescope and headlight reflectors (parabolas) and more.
Rotate a line (generator) about a fixed line (axis) that it meets at the vertex V, keeping the angle α between them fixed: this gives a double-napped cone with semi-vertical angle α.
Let the cutting plane make angle β with the axis (not through V): β = 90° gives a circle; α < β < 90° an ellipse; β = α a parabola; 0 ≤ β < α a hyperbola (cutting both nappes).
If the plane passes through the vertex: α < β ≤ 90° gives a point; β = α gives a straight line (a generator); 0 ≤ β < α gives a pair of intersecting lines. These are degenerate conics.
Planets move in ellipses with the Sun at one focus (Kepler); car headlights and satellite dishes are parabolic.

example.q: A double cone has semi-vertical angle 30°. A plane not through the vertex makes an angle of 50° with the axis. What curve is formed?
steps: α < β < 90°, so the section is an ellipse.

learn.reallife: ISRO's Mangalyaan travelled on an elliptical transfer orbit before Mars captured it — orbital mechanics is conic sections in action.

games.title: Which conic? (α = semi-vertical angle, β = angle of plane with axis, plane not through vertex)

quiz.q: A plane perpendicular to the axis of the cone (not through the vertex) cuts it in a:
quiz.explain: β = 90° gives a circle.
steps: Perpendicular to the axis means β = 90°
β = 90° (plane not through V) gives a circle
quiz.mistake: Confuses 'perpendicular to the axis' with 'parallel to a generator'

quiz.q: When the cutting plane is parallel to a generator (β = α, plane not through vertex), the section is a:
quiz.explain: β = α gives a parabola, which is open and has one branch.
steps: Plane parallel to a generator: β = α
β = α (not through V) gives a parabola
A parabola is open with one branch
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the parabola and hyperbola conditions

quiz.q: Which section cuts BOTH nappes of the cone?
quiz.explain: When β < α the plane is steep enough to meet both nappes, giving a hyperbola with two branches.
steps: Both nappes are cut when the plane is steeper than the generator: β < α
Its two branches lie on the two nappes
quiz.mistake: Thinks the parabola has two branches

quiz.q: If the plane passes through the vertex and α < β ≤ 90°, the section is:
quiz.explain: The plane meets the cone only at the vertex — a degenerate conic.
steps: Plane through the vertex with α < β ≤ 90°
It meets the cone only at the vertex V
quiz.mistake: Forgets the degenerate cases

quiz.q: The semi-vertical angle of a cone is the angle between:
options: the cutting plane and the axis
quiz.explain: α is fixed as the generator rotates about the axis.
steps: The cone is formed by rotating a generator about the axis
The fixed angle α between them is the semi-vertical angle
It is not the angle with the cutting plane or the base
α = angle between the axis and a generator
Answer: the axis and a generator
quiz.mistake: Confuses α with β

quiz.q: Which real-life object uses a parabola's shape?
quiz.explain: A bulb at the focus of a parabolic reflector sends light out in a parallel beam.
steps: A bulb at the focus of a parabolic reflector sends light out as a parallel beam
Planet orbits are ellipses; wheels are circles
quiz.mistake: Thinks planetary orbits are parabolic

quiz.q: For α = 45° and β = 60° (plane not through the vertex), the section is:
quiz.explain: 45° < 60° < 90°, so it is an ellipse.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the inequality between α and β

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The path of the Earth around the Sun is an ellipse.
Reason (R): An ellipse is obtained when the cutting plane is perpendicular to the axis of the cone.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true (Kepler's first law). R is false: a plane perpendicular to the axis gives a circle; an ellipse needs α < β < 90°.
steps: A: Earth's orbit is an ellipse (Kepler's first law) → true
R: a plane perpendicular to the axis (β = 90°) gives a circle, not an ellipse
Answer: A is true but R is false
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the conditions for circle and ellipse

teach.ask: Gappu has an ice-cream cone and a knife. Explain how slicing a double cone at different angles gives a circle, ellipse, parabola and hyperbola.
teach.praise: Straight across — circle; tilted — ellipse; parallel to the side — parabola; steep — hyperbola! Tasty maths.
teach.nudge: What happens when the plane is parallel to a generator?

revise.summary: Conic sections are the curves made when a plane cuts a double cone with semi-vertical angle α. Comparing the plane's angle β with the axis gives a circle (β = 90°), ellipse (α < β < 90°), parabola (β = α) or hyperbola (β < α).
focus: Identify the conic from α and β
Name the degenerate conics when the plane passes through the vertex
Link conics to real uses: orbits (ellipse), reflectors (parabola)
remember: β = 90°: circle; α < β < 90°: ellipse; β = α: parabola; 0 ≤ β < α: hyperbola
Plane through the vertex: point (α < β ≤ 90°), line (β = α), pair of lines (β < α)
Semi-vertical angle α: angle between the axis and a generator
traps: A plane perpendicular to the axis gives a circle, not an ellipse
Only the hyperbola cuts both nappes of the cone

learn.hook: A cricket ground's boundary rope is a circle around the pitch — every point at the same distance from the centre. Write that as an equation and you've got (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r².
points: A circle is the set of all points in a plane at a fixed distance r (radius) from a fixed point (centre).
Centre (h, k), radius r: (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r². Centre at the origin: x² + y² = r².
General form x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 has centre (−g, −f) and radius √(g² + f² − c), when g² + f² − c > 0.
Completing squares is the safe method: group x-terms and y-terms and add the right constants.
The coefficients of x² and y² must be equal (and there is no xy term); divide through if they are equal but not 1.

example.q: Find the centre and radius of x² + y² − 6x + 4y − 12 = 0.

learn.reallife: A Chennai lighthouse's beam that reaches 20 km out covers the circle x² + y² = 400 (in km) on a map centred at the lighthouse.

games.title: Complete the square for x² + y² + 8x − 10y − 8 = 0

quiz.q: The equation of the circle with centre (−2, 3) and radius 4 is:
steps: (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r² with (h, k) = (−2, 3), r = 4
quiz.mistake: Uses (x − 2) and (y + 3), flipping the centre's signs

quiz.q: What is the radius of x² + y² − 4x − 8y − 5 = 0?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to add the completed-square constants

quiz.q: What is the centre of 2x² + 2y² − 8x + 12y − 6 = 0?
quiz.explain: Divide by 2: x² + y² − 4x + 6y − 3 = 0, so centre (−g, −f) = (2, −3).
quiz.mistake: Forgets to divide by 2 first

quiz.q: The radius of 2x² + 2y² − 8x + 12y − 6 = 0 is:
quiz.explain: After dividing by 2: r = √(4 + 9 + 3) = √16 = 4.
steps: After dividing by 2: g = −2, f = 3, c = −3
quiz.mistake: Uses c = −6 without dividing by 2

quiz.q: Which equation represents a circle?
quiz.explain: A circle needs equal x² and y² coefficients and no xy term. x² + y² + 2x = 0 is (x + 1)² + y² = 1.
steps: A circle needs equal x² and y² coefficients and no xy term
x² + 2y² has unequal coefficients; xy term appears in one; x² − y² has opposite signs
quiz.mistake: Accepts unequal coefficients

quiz.q: The circle with centre at the origin and radius 6 is:
quiz.explain: x² + y² = r² = 36.
steps: Centre at the origin: x² + y² = r²
quiz.mistake: Forgets to square the radius

quiz.q: For what value of k is x² + y² − 6x + 8y + k = 0 a circle of radius 5?
quiz.mistake: Sets k = r²

quiz.q: The circle (x − 1)² + (y − 1)² = 1 touches:
quiz.explain: The centre (1, 1) is at distance 1 from both axes, equal to the radius.
steps: Distance from the centre to the x-axis = 1 = r, so it touches the x-axis
Distance to the y-axis = 1 = r, so it touches the y-axis too
The circle touches both coordinate axes
quiz.mistake: Checks only one axis

teach.ask: Gappu found x² + y² − 6x + 4y − 12 = 0 in his book and can't spot the circle. Explain how to find the centre and radius.
teach.praise: Group, complete the squares, and read off (3, −2) and 5. The circle was hiding in plain sight!
teach.nudge: What constant must you add to x² − 6x to make a perfect square?

revise.summary: A circle with centre (h, k) and radius r is (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r². The general form x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 has centre (−g, −f) and radius √(g² + f² − c).
focus: Write the equation of a circle from its centre and radius
Find the centre and radius from the general form, by completing squares
Recognise when an equation is a circle
Divide through when the x² and y² coefficients are equal but not 1
remember: (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r²; centre at origin: x² + y² = r²
x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0: centre (−g, −f), radius √(g² + f² − c)
A circle needs equal x² and y² coefficients and no xy term
traps: The centre is (−g, −f): change the signs of half the x and y coefficients
Divide by the x² coefficient first (e.g. by 2) before reading g, f and c

learn.hook: Three ATM machines on a map — is there a circle through all of them? Conditions like 'passes through these points' or 'centre on this line' pin down a circle.
points: Start with (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r² or x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0, and use each condition to write an equation.
Through two points with centre on a given line: the centre is equidistant from both points (and on the line). Solve for (h, k), then r.
Through three points: substitute each into the general form to get three linear equations in g, f, c.
Position of a point (x₁, y₁) relative to x² + y² = r²: inside if x₁² + y₁² < r², on if =, outside if >.
A circle through the origin has c = 0 in the general form.

example.q: Find the circle through (0, 0) and (4, 0) whose centre lies on the line y = x.
steps: Centre (h, h). Equal distances to (0, 0) and (4, 0): h² + h² = (h − 4)² + h² ⇒ h² = h² − 8h + 16 ⇒ h = 2.

learn.reallife: Earthquake epicentres are located by drawing circles around three seismograph stations and finding where they meet.

games.title: Inside, on or outside x² + y² = 25?
Circle through (0, 0), (6, 0), (0, 8)
items: Then (6, 0) gives 36 + 12g = 0, so g = −3, and (0, 8) gives 64 + 16f = 0, so f = −4

quiz.q: The circle through (0, 0), (a, 0) and (0, b) is:
quiz.explain: c = 0 from the origin; (a, 0) gives a² + 2ga = 0 ⇒ 2g = −a; similarly 2f = −b.
steps: Through (0, 0): c = 0 in x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0
quiz.mistake: Gets the signs of g and f wrong

quiz.q: Is the point (2.5, −4) inside, on or outside the circle x² + y² = 25?
quiz.mistake: Compares the coordinates with 5 directly

quiz.q: A circle passes through (1, 0) and (0, 3), and its centre lies on the line x − y = 1. Its centre is:
quiz.explain: Equal distances: (h − 1)² + k² = h² + (k − 3)² ⇒ h − 3k = −4. With h − k = 1: k = 5/2, h = 7/2.
quiz.mistake: Solves the simultaneous equations with a sign slip

quiz.q: A circle of radius 5 has its centre on the y-axis and passes through (3, 2). Which can be its centre?
steps: Centre on the y-axis: (0, k); radius 5
quiz.mistake: Takes the centre at (0, 5)

quiz.q: The circle x² + y² − 6x − 8y = 0 passes through which point?
options: (6, 0) and nothing else on the axes
quiz.explain: There is no constant term, so (0, 0) satisfies it. (3, 4) is the centre.
steps: x² + y² − 6x − 8y = 0 has no constant term (c = 0)
(3, 4) is the centre, not on the circle
quiz.mistake: Confuses the centre with a point on the circle

quiz.q: How many circles pass through three given non-collinear points?
quiz.explain: Three non-collinear points fix g, f and c uniquely — this is the circumcircle.
steps: Three points give three equations in g, f, c
If the points are not collinear, these have exactly one solution
quiz.mistake: Thinks three points allow many circles

quiz.q: The circle with centre (2, 2) passing through the origin has radius:
steps: Radius = distance from the centre (2, 2) to the origin
quiz.mistake: Takes r = 2

quiz.q: If (k, 1) lies on x² + y² = 10 and k > 0, then k is:
quiz.mistake: Forgets to subtract 1

teach.ask: Gappu knows a circle passes through two points and its centre is on a line. Explain how to find the circle, and how to test if a point is inside it.
teach.praise: Equal distances to both points plus the line gives the centre. And x² + y² < r² means inside!
teach.nudge: What is special about the distances from the centre to the two given points?

revise.summary: To find a circle from conditions, start from (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r² or the general form and turn each condition into an equation. A point is inside, on or outside x² + y² = r² as x₁² + y₁² is less than, equal to or greater than r².
focus: Find a circle through given points, or with its centre on a given line
Decide whether a point is inside, on or outside a circle
Use c = 0 for circles through the origin
remember: Each condition gives one equation in h, k, r (or g, f, c)
x₁² + y₁² < r²: inside; = r²: on; > r²: outside
A circle through the origin has c = 0
Exactly one circle passes through three non-collinear points
traps: Don't forget the second solution when solving (2 − k)² = 16: k = 6 or k = −2
The centre of a circle is not a point on the circle

learn.hook: Throw a ball, aim a TV dish, design a headlight — all parabolas. Every point on one is exactly as far from a point (focus) as from a line (directrix).
points: A parabola is the set of points equidistant from a fixed line (directrix) and a fixed point (focus) not on it.
Axis: the line through the focus perpendicular to the directrix. Vertex: where the parabola meets its axis. Latus rectum: the chord through the focus perpendicular to the axis.
y² = 4ax: focus (a, 0), directrix x = −a, axis the x-axis, opens right. y² = −4ax: focus (−a, 0), directrix x = a, opens left.
x² = 4ay: focus (0, a), directrix y = −a, opens up. x² = −4ay: focus (0, −a), directrix y = a, opens down. (a > 0 throughout.)
Length of the latus rectum = 4a.

example.q: Find the focus, axis, directrix and latus rectum length of y² = 20x.
example.answer: Focus (5, 0), axis y = 0, directrix x = −5, latus rectum 20

learn.reallife: The big radio telescope dishes (such as GMRT near Pune) are parabolic: incoming parallel signals all bounce to the receiver at the focus.

games.title: Read a from the equation and give the latus rectum length

quiz.q: The focus of x² = −20y is:
quiz.explain: x² = −4ay with 4a = 20 ⇒ a = 5; focus (0, −a) = (0, −5).
quiz.mistake: Ignores the minus sign

quiz.q: The directrix of y² = 14x is:
quiz.explain: 4a = 14 ⇒ a = 7/2; directrix x = −a.
quiz.mistake: Uses 4a instead of a

quiz.q: The length of the latus rectum of x² = 10y is:
quiz.explain: Latus rectum = 4a and here 4a = 10.
quiz.mistake: Gives a = 5/2 instead of 4a

quiz.q: Which parabola has its focus at (0, 3)?
quiz.explain: Focus (0, a) with a = 3 means x² = 4ay = 12y.
steps: Focus (0, 3) is on the positive y-axis → form x² = 4ay
quiz.mistake: Uses 4a = 3

quiz.q: A point on y² = 4ax is at distance 7 from the directrix x = −3. Its distance from the focus is:
quiz.explain: For every point on a parabola, distance to focus = distance to directrix.
steps: Definition: every point is equidistant from the focus and the directrix
So distance to the focus is also 7
quiz.mistake: Subtracts a from the distance

quiz.q: The parabola y² = −8x opens:
quiz.explain: y² = −4ax (a = 2) has focus (−2, 0), so it opens towards negative x.
steps: A parabola opens towards its focus
quiz.mistake: Thinks y² always opens to the right

quiz.q: Which statement about the parabola y² = 4ax (a > 0) is false?
quiz.explain: The axis of y² = 4ax is the x-axis (y = 0).
steps: For y² = 4ax: focus (a, 0), latus rectum 4a, vertex (0, 0) are all true
The axis is the line through the focus and vertex: y = 0, the x-axis
So 'its axis is the y-axis' is wrong
The false statement: its axis is the y-axis
Answer: Its axis is the y-axis
quiz.mistake: Confuses the axis with the directrix direction

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Every point of a parabola is equidistant from its focus and directrix.
Reason (R): The vertex of y² = 4ax lies midway between the focus (a, 0) and the directrix x = −a.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true. R is a consequence of A applied to one point (the vertex), not the explanation of A, which is the definition itself.
steps: A is the definition of a parabola, so A is true
R: vertex (0, 0) is a from both the focus (a, 0) and the directrix x = −a, so R is true
R is just A applied to one point, not the reason for A
Answer: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Treats a special case as the reason for the definition

teach.ask: Gappu wants to know what makes a curve a parabola and how to read its focus and directrix from y² = 20x. Explain.
teach.praise: Same distance from a point and a line — that's a parabola. And y² = 20x means a = 5. Dish aimed!
teach.nudge: Every point on a parabola is equally far from which two things?

revise.summary: A parabola is the set of points equidistant from a focus and a directrix. Its four standard forms are y² = ±4ax and x² = ±4ay (a > 0), each with vertex at the origin and latus rectum of length 4a.
focus: Find the focus, directrix, axis and latus rectum from a standard equation
Tell which way a parabola opens from its form
Use 'distance to focus = distance to directrix' for points on a parabola
remember: y² = 4ax: focus (a, 0), directrix x = −a, opens right; y² = −4ax opens left
x² = 4ay: focus (0, a), directrix y = −a, opens up; x² = −4ay opens down
Latus rectum length = 4a
Any point on the parabola: distance to focus = distance to directrix
traps: Find a from 4a: in y² = 14x, a = 7/2, not 14
The axis of y² = 4ax is the x-axis, not the y-axis

learn.hook: Engineers designing a headlight need to know exactly where the bulb goes. Give them the depth and width of the reflector and the parabola's focus tells them.
points: From an equation: match it to one of the four standard forms, find a, then read the focus, axis, directrix and latus rectum.
From focus and directrix (vertex at origin): the focus tells the form; e.g. focus (7, 0) and directrix x = −7 give y² = 28x.
From vertex (0, 0) and focus: focus (0, −5) gives x² = −20y.
Through a point with a given axis: substitute the point to find a; e.g. y² = 4ax through (3, 6) gives 36 = 12a, so a = 3.
Applications: headlight and dish reflectors (bulb or receiver at the focus), parabolic arches, and cables of suspension bridges under uniform load.

example.q: A dish reflector is 24 cm wide and 4 cm deep at its centre. How far from the vertex is the focus?
steps: Place the vertex at the origin with the axis along the y-axis: x² = 4ay.

learn.reallife: The main cables of a suspension bridge carrying a uniformly loaded deck hang very nearly in the shape of a parabola.

games.title: Equation of the parabola with vertex (0, 0), axis along x-axis, through (3, 6)

quiz.q: The parabola with focus (0, −6) and directrix y = 6 is:
quiz.explain: a = 6 and the focus is below the vertex, so x² = −4ay = −24y.
steps: Focus (0, −6) and directrix y = 6: vertex at the origin, a = 6
quiz.mistake: Ignores the side of the focus

quiz.q: The parabola with vertex (0, 0), axis along the y-axis, passing through (2, 3) is:
steps: Axis along the y-axis, vertex (0, 0): x² = 4ay
quiz.mistake: Substitutes into y² = 4ax instead

quiz.q: A parabolic dish is 16 cm wide and 4 cm deep at its centre. How far from the vertex is its focus?
quiz.explain: x² = 4ay through (8, 4): 64 = 16a ⇒ a = 4 cm.
steps: Vertex at the origin; rim point (16/2, 4) = (8, 4) on x² = 4ay
Focus is 4 cm from the vertex
quiz.mistake: Uses the full width 16 instead of half the width

quiz.q: The focus of x² = 9y lies at:
quiz.mistake: Takes a = 9

quiz.q: An equilateral triangle is inscribed in y² = 4ax with one vertex at the origin. Its side is 8a√3. For y² = 4x, the side is:
quiz.explain: Here a = 1, so the side is 8√3. (The other vertices are (12a, ±4√3 a).)
steps: Side of the equilateral triangle in y² = 4ax = 8a√3
quiz.mistake: Uses 4a instead of a

quiz.q: The latus rectum of the parabola through (−3, 6) with vertex at the origin and axis along the x-axis has length:
quiz.explain: y² = 4ax through (−3, 6): 36 = −12a, so a = −3 and the parabola is y² = −12x. The latus rectum is 4|a| = 12.
quiz.mistake: Takes 4a as 6

quiz.q: Why is the bulb of a car headlight placed at the focus of the parabolic reflector?
options: Light from the focus reflects off the parabola into a beam parallel to the axis
The focus is the hottest point
Light from the focus spreads in all directions
The focus is the deepest point
quiz.explain: This reflective property of the parabola turns a point source into a parallel beam.
steps: Reflective property: a ray from the focus reflects off a parabola parallel to its axis
So a bulb at the focus gives a straight, parallel beam
That is why headlights put the bulb there
Answer: Light from the focus reflects off the parabola into a beam parallel to the axis
quiz.mistake: Thinks the focus is the vertex

quiz.q: Which parabola has its directrix x = 4 and vertex at the origin?
quiz.explain: Directrix x = a for y² = −4ax with a = 4, so y² = −16x.
steps: Directrix x = 4 is to the right of the vertex, so the focus is (−4, 0)
quiz.mistake: Uses directrix x = −a

teach.ask: Gappu is building a solar cooker with a parabolic dish 24 cm wide and 4 cm deep. Explain how to find where to put the cooking pot (the focus).
teach.praise: Put the rim point into x² = 4ay, find a, and the pot goes a cm above the vertex. Dinner's cooking!
teach.nudge: Which point on the dish do you substitute into the equation?

revise.summary: To solve parabola problems, match the equation to a standard form and find a, or build the equation from the focus, directrix, axis or a given point. Reflectors place the bulb or receiver at the focus.
focus: Write a parabola from its focus and directrix or vertex and focus
Find a parabola with a given axis through a point
Solve dish and reflector problems using x² = 4ay through a rim point
remember: Focus (a, 0), directrix x = −a → y² = 4ax; focus (0, −a), directrix y = a → x² = −4ay
Through a point: substitute it to find a
Dish of width w and depth d: rim point (w/2, d) on x² = 4ay; focus at distance a from the vertex
Light from the focus reflects into a beam parallel to the axis
traps: Use half the width of a dish as the x-coordinate of the rim point
A negative a from substitution means the parabola opens the other way; the latus rectum is 4|a|

topics.title: Ellipse: definition, parts and standard form

learn.hook: Tie a string to two pins, pull it tight with a pencil and draw: you get an ellipse. The sum of distances to the two pins never changes.
points: An ellipse is the set of points whose distances from two fixed points (foci) have a constant sum, 2a.
Centre: midpoint of the foci. Major axis (length 2a) passes through the foci; minor axis (length 2b) is perpendicular to it. c = distance from centre to a focus, and c² = a² − b².
Major axis along x-axis: x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 (a > b), foci (±c, 0), vertices (±a, 0). Along y-axis: x²/b² + y²/a² = 1, foci (0, ±c).
Derivation: from PF₁ + PF₂ = 2a with F₁(−c, 0), F₂(c, 0), isolate one root, square twice and use b² = a² − c².
Eccentricity e = c/a, and 0 < e < 1. As e → 0 the ellipse becomes nearly a circle.

example.q: For x²/25 + y²/9 = 1, find a, b, c, the foci and the eccentricity.
steps: a² = 25, b² = 9 (larger denominator under x², so major axis on the x-axis).

learn.reallife: Earth's orbit is an ellipse with e ≈ 0.017 — so nearly circular that the Earth–Sun distance changes by only about 3% over a year.

games.title: Derive the ellipse equation
items: Take foci F₁(−c, 0), F₂(c, 0) and PF₁ + PF₂ = 2a
Square and simplify: a − (c/a)x = √((x − c)² + y²)
Square again: x²(a² − c²)/a² + y² = a² − c²
Put b² = a² − c²: x²/a² + y²/b² = 1

quiz.q: For x²/16 + y²/25 = 1, the major axis lies along:
quiz.explain: 25 > 16 and 25 is under y², so a² = 25 lies along the y-axis.
steps: It sits under y², so the major axis is vertical
quiz.mistake: Assumes the major axis is always on the x-axis

quiz.q: The foci of x²/16 + y²/25 = 1 are:
quiz.explain: c² = 25 − 16 = 9, c = 3, along the major (y) axis.
steps: Foci lie on the major (y) axis
quiz.mistake: Adds a² and b² as for a hyperbola

quiz.q: The eccentricity of x²/169 + y²/144 = 1 is:
quiz.mistake: Uses b/a

quiz.q: A point P is on an ellipse with foci F₁, F₂ and major axis length 10. What is PF₁ + PF₂?
quiz.explain: By definition the sum is constant and equals 2a = the major axis length.
steps: Definition: PF₁ + PF₂ = 2a for every point P
It does not depend on P
quiz.mistake: Thinks the sum changes with P

quiz.q: Which value can the eccentricity of an ellipse take?
quiz.explain: For an ellipse 0 < e < 1.
steps: 1 and 1.5 are too large; −0.5 is negative
quiz.mistake: Thinks e can be 1 or more

quiz.q: For an ellipse with a = 5 and c = 3, what is b?
steps: c² = a² − b² → b² = a² − c²
quiz.mistake: Uses b² = a² + c²

quiz.q: The length of the minor axis of 16x² + 25y² = 400 is:
quiz.explain: x²/25 + y²/16 = 1: b = 4, minor axis 2b = 8.
quiz.mistake: Gives b instead of 2b

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): In an ellipse, a > c.
Reason (R): The sum of the distances of any point from the foci, 2a, is greater than the distance between the foci, 2c.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: For any point P not on the segment F₁F₂, PF₁ + PF₂ > F₁F₂ (triangle inequality), so 2a > 2c. R explains A.
steps: R: for P not on segment F₁F₂, PF₁ + PF₂ > F₁F₂ (triangle inequality), so 2a > 2c: true
Dividing by 2 gives a > c, which is A
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not see why a must exceed c

teach.ask: Gappu drew a curve with two pins and a string. Explain why it's an ellipse and what a, b, c and e mean.
teach.praise: Two pins, a fixed sum, and c² = a² − b². And e < 1 always. Pin-tastic!
teach.nudge: What stays the same as the pencil moves around the two pins?

revise.summary: An ellipse is the set of points whose distances from two foci add up to 2a. With major axis along the x-axis it is x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 (a > b), foci (±c, 0), c² = a² − b², and eccentricity e = c/a with 0 < e < 1.
focus: Find a, b, c, foci, vertices and e from a standard equation
Decide the direction of the major axis from the larger denominator
Use PF₁ + PF₂ = 2a and c² = a² − b²
remember: PF₁ + PF₂ = 2a (constant)
x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 (a > b): foci (±c, 0), vertices (±a, 0); x²/b² + y²/a² = 1: foci (0, ±c)
c² = a² − b²; e = c/a, 0 < e < 1
traps: The larger denominator is a², whether it is under x² or y²
For an ellipse c² = a² − b²; don't add as in a hyperbola

learn.hook: Ellipse questions in board exams are 'read off everything' or 'build from clues'. Master a, b, c and these become free marks.
points: Latus rectum: a chord through a focus perpendicular to the major axis; its length is 2b²/a.
From an equation: write it as x²/A + y²/B = 1. The larger denominator is a² and tells the direction of the major axis. Then c, foci, vertices, e and latus rectum follow.
From clues: vertices give a, foci give c, and b² = a² − c². Ends of the minor axis give b.
Through a point: substitute it into x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 to get a relation.
Rod sliding between the axes: if a point P on a rod AB (A on the x-axis, B on the y-axis) has PA = p and PB = q, P traces x²/q² + y²/p² = 1.

example.q: Find the equation of the ellipse with vertices (±10, 0) and foci (±6, 0).

learn.reallife: The arches of many old bridges and the 'whispering galleries' of some domes are elliptical: a whisper at one focus is heard clearly at the other.

games.title: Clues ↔ ellipse
pairs: Ends of major axis (±3, 0), minor axis (0, ±2)
Rod 10 cm, PA = 4 cm, PB = 6 cm

quiz.q: The length of the latus rectum of x²/36 + y²/16 = 1 is:
quiz.mistake: Uses 2a²/b

quiz.q: The ellipse with foci (0, ±5) and major axis 26 has equation:
quiz.explain: a = 13, c = 5, b² = 169 − 25 = 144. Major axis on the y-axis, so a² goes under y².
steps: Major axis 26 → a = 13; foci (0, ±5) → c = 5, on the y-axis
quiz.mistake: Puts a² under x² though the foci are on the y-axis

quiz.q: The eccentricity of 9x² + 25y² = 225 is:
quiz.mistake: Uses b/a = 3/5

quiz.q: An ellipse with centre at the origin and major axis on the x-axis passes through (2, 3) and (4, 1). What is a²?
quiz.mistake: Solves the linear system with a slip

quiz.q: A rod of length 15 cm moves with its ends on the axes. The point P on it with PA = 5 cm (A on the x-axis) traces:
quiz.explain: PB = 10 cm, and P traces x²/PB² + y²/PA² = 1, i.e. x²/100 + y²/25 = 1.
steps: PA = 5 cm, rod 15 cm → PB = 10 cm
quiz.mistake: Swaps the two distances

quiz.q: The vertices of x²/49 + y²/36 = 1 are:
quiz.explain: a² = 49 under x², so vertices are (±a, 0) = (±7, 0).
steps: a² = 49 is the larger denominator, under x²
Major axis on the x-axis, a = 7
quiz.mistake: Gives the foci or the minor-axis ends

quiz.q: An elliptical arch spans 8 m at its base and is 2 m high at the centre. How high is it 2 m from the centre?
steps: Base 8 m → a = 4; height 2 m → b = 2: x²/16 + y²/4 = 1
quiz.mistake: Uses the full span 8 as a

quiz.q: For an ellipse, the distance between the foci is 8 and the minor axis is 6. What is the major axis length?
quiz.explain: c = 4, b = 3, a² = b² + c² = 25 ⇒ a = 5; major axis 2a = 10.
steps: Distance between foci 2c = 8 → c = 4; minor axis 2b = 6 → b = 3
quiz.mistake: Gives a instead of 2a

teach.ask: Gappu's question gives vertices (±10, 0) and foci (±6, 0). Explain how to build the ellipse equation and find its latus rectum.
teach.praise: Vertices give a, foci give c, then b² = a² − c². And the latus rectum is 2b²/a. Equation built!
teach.nudge: Once you know a and c, how do you get b?

revise.summary: For ellipse problems, the larger denominator is a² and fixes the major axis; vertices give a, foci give c, and b² = a² − c². The latus rectum has length 2b²/a.
focus: Read foci, vertices, e and latus rectum from any ellipse equation
Build the equation from vertices, foci or axis lengths
Solve arch and sliding-rod problems
remember: Latus rectum length = 2b²/a
b² = a² − c²
Rod with PA = p (A on x-axis) and PB = q: P traces x²/q² + y²/p² = 1
traps: Put a² under y² when the foci are on the y-axis
Divide by the constant on the right first, e.g. 9x² + 25y² = 225 → x²/25 + y²/9 = 1

topics.title: Hyperbola: definition, parts and standard form

learn.hook: Hear a thunderclap at two places a known time apart and you know the difference of your distances from the lightning — so it lies on a hyperbola.
points: A hyperbola is the set of points whose distances from two fixed points (foci) have a constant difference, 2a (taken as positive).
Transverse axis: through the foci, length 2a between the vertices. Conjugate axis: perpendicular, length 2b. c = centre-to-focus distance, and c² = a² + b².
Transverse axis on x-axis: x²/a² − y²/b² = 1, foci (±c, 0), vertices (±a, 0). On y-axis: y²/a² − x²/b² = 1, foci (0, ±c).
Derivation: from |PF₁ − PF₂| = 2a, square twice and use b² = c² − a².
Eccentricity e = c/a > 1 (since c > a). Unlike the ellipse, a need not be larger than b.

example.q: For x²/25 − y²/144 = 1, find the foci, vertices and eccentricity.
steps: a² = 25, b² = 144 (the positive term is under x², so the transverse axis is the x-axis).

learn.reallife: Hyperbolic paths appear in long-range radio navigation: a receiver measuring the time difference of signals from two stations lies on a hyperbola.

games.title: Derive the hyperbola equation
items: Foci F₁(−c, 0), F₂(c, 0) and PF₁ − PF₂ = 2a
Square and simplify: (c/a)x − a = √((x − c)² + y²)
Square again: x²(c² − a²)/a² − y² = c² − a²
Put b² = c² − a²: x²/a² − y²/b² = 1

quiz.q: For y²/36 − x²/64 = 1, the foci are:
quiz.explain: c² = 36 + 64 = 100, c = 10, on the y-axis (the positive term is y²).
steps: Positive term y²: transverse axis on the y-axis, a² = 36, b² = 64
quiz.mistake: Subtracts as for an ellipse

quiz.q: The eccentricity of x²/9 − y²/16 = 1 is:
quiz.mistake: Uses c² = a² − b²

quiz.q: Which value can the eccentricity of a hyperbola take?
quiz.explain: For a hyperbola e > 1.
quiz.mistake: Confuses with an ellipse

quiz.q: The length of the transverse axis of 16x² − 9y² = 144 is:
quiz.explain: x²/9 − y²/16 = 1: a = 3, transverse axis 2a = 6.
quiz.mistake: Gives the conjugate axis 2b = 8

quiz.q: For a point on a hyperbola with vertices (±4, 0), the difference of its distances from the foci is:
quiz.explain: |PF₁ − PF₂| = 2a = 8, the distance between the vertices.
steps: Definition: |PF₁ − PF₂| = 2a for every point P
quiz.mistake: Gives a instead of 2a

quiz.q: For a hyperbola, which relation is correct?
quiz.explain: For a hyperbola the foci lie beyond the vertices, and c² = a² + b².
steps: The foci lie beyond the vertices, so c > a
quiz.mistake: Uses the ellipse relation

quiz.q: Which equation is a hyperbola with transverse axis along the y-axis?
quiz.explain: The positive term is under y², so the transverse axis is the y-axis.
steps: Transverse axis along the y-axis needs the positive term to be y²: y²/a² − x²/b² = 1
x²/4 − y²/9 = 1 has a positive x² term; the others are an ellipse and a parabola
quiz.mistake: Looks at the larger denominator instead of the positive term

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): For x²/4 − y²/9 = 1, b > a is allowed.
Reason (R): In a hyperbola, a is always greater than b.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Here a = 2, b = 3 and it is a valid hyperbola, so A is true. R is false: only c > a is required; b can be larger or smaller than a.
steps: x²/4 − y²/9 = 1: a = 2, b = 3, and it is a valid hyperbola, so A is true
R claims a > b always, but here b > a
A hyperbola only needs c > a, so R is false
Answer: A is true but R is false
quiz.mistake: Carries over the ellipse rule a > b

teach.ask: Gappu confuses the ellipse and hyperbola formulas. Explain the hyperbola's definition, c² = a² + b², and why e > 1.
teach.praise: Ellipse adds distances, hyperbola subtracts them — and c² = a² + b² so e > 1. No more mix-ups!
teach.nudge: For a hyperbola, is it the sum or the difference of focal distances that stays constant?

revise.summary: A hyperbola is the set of points whose distances from two foci differ by 2a. With transverse axis along the x-axis it is x²/a² − y²/b² = 1, foci (±c, 0), c² = a² + b², and eccentricity e = c/a > 1.
focus: Find a, b, c, foci, vertices and e from a standard equation
Decide the transverse axis from the positive term
Use |PF₁ − PF₂| = 2a and c² = a² + b²
remember: |PF₁ − PF₂| = 2a (constant)
x²/a² − y²/b² = 1: foci (±c, 0), vertices (±a, 0); y²/a² − x²/b² = 1: foci (0, ±c)
c² = a² + b²; e = c/a > 1
a need not be larger than b
traps: For a hyperbola c² = a² + b², not a² − b²
The positive term decides the transverse axis, not the larger denominator

topics.title: Hyperbola problems and mixed conic problems

learn.hook: Board papers love a 'find everything' hyperbola question and a twist problem mixing parabolas and real objects. Let's practise both.
points: Latus rectum of a hyperbola: length 2b²/a.
From an equation: bring it to x²/a² − y²/b² = 1 or y²/a² − x²/b² = 1; the positive term gives the transverse axis.
From clues: vertices give a, foci give c, b² = c² − a². A given transverse/conjugate axis gives 2a or 2b.
Through a point: substitute it to find the unknown.
Mixed problems: parabolic cables and dishes (use the vertex as origin and a rim or support point), and triangles inscribed in parabolas.

example.q: Find the hyperbola with foci (±10, 0) and transverse axis of length 12.

learn.reallife: The cooling towers of many thermal power stations have a hyperbolic profile — strong and material-saving.

quiz.q: The hyperbola with vertices (0, ±4) and foci (0, ±5) is:
quiz.explain: a = 4, c = 5, b² = 25 − 16 = 9; transverse axis on the y-axis.
steps: Vertices (0, ±4) → a = 4; foci (0, ±5) → c = 5; both on the y-axis
quiz.mistake: Swaps a² and b²

quiz.q: The latus rectum length of x²/16 − y²/9 = 1 is:
quiz.mistake: Uses 2a²/b

quiz.q: Find the hyperbola with foci (0, ±10) and conjugate axis of length 16.
quiz.explain: b = 8, c = 10, a² = 100 − 64 = 36; foci on the y-axis.
quiz.mistake: Uses c² for a²

quiz.q: Find a² if the hyperbola x²/a² − y²/4 = 1 passes through (3, 2).
quiz.mistake: Forgets the −y²/b² term

quiz.q: The vertices of 4y² − 9x² = 36 are:
quiz.explain: Divide by 36: y²/9 − x²/4 = 1, so a = 3 on the y-axis.
quiz.mistake: Reads a from the x² term

quiz.q: A parabolic suspension cable hangs between towers 100 m apart; it is 30 m above the road at the towers and 10 m at the centre. Taking the lowest point as (0, 0), the cable is x² = 4ay through (50, 20). What is 4a?
steps: Lowest point (0, 0); tower top 50 m across and 30 − 10 = 20 m up: (50, 20)
quiz.mistake: Uses the full height 30 m instead of 30 − 10 = 20 m

quiz.q: A satellite dish is 1 m wide and 0.125 m deep at the centre. Its receiver is placed at the focus. How far is it from the vertex?
steps: Vertex at the origin; rim point (1/2, 0.125) = (0.5, 0.125)
Receiver is 0.5 m from the vertex
quiz.mistake: Uses the full width as x

quiz.q: The foci of x²/16 − y²/9 = 1 and of the ellipse x²/25 + y²/9 = 1 compare as:
quiz.explain: Hyperbola: c² = 16 + 9 = 25. Ellipse: c² = 25 − 9 = 16.
steps: Hyperbola x²/16 − y²/9 = 1: c² = a² + b² = 16 + 9 = 25 → c = 5
Ellipse x²/25 + y²/9 = 1: c² = a² − b² = 25 − 9 = 16 → c = 4
quiz.mistake: Uses the same rule for both curves

teach.ask: Gappu gets 'foci (±10, 0), transverse axis 12' and must write the hyperbola. Explain the steps and how to find its latus rectum.
teach.praise: 2a from the transverse axis, c from the foci, b² = c² − a². Then 2b²/a. Hyperbola done!
teach.nudge: How is b² found for a hyperbola — c² + a² or c² − a²?

revise.summary: For hyperbola problems, write the equation in standard form; the positive term fixes the transverse axis, vertices give a, foci give c, and b² = c² − a². The latus rectum has length 2b²/a; parabolic cables and dishes are solved with x² = 4ay.
focus: Build hyperbola equations from vertices, foci and axis lengths
Find the latus rectum and unknowns from a point on the curve

b² = c² − a² for a hyperbola (b² = a² − c² for an ellipse)
Through a point: substitute it to find the unknown

learn.hook: To tell an electrician exactly where a bulb hangs in a room, you need three numbers: how far along, how far across, and how high. Welcome to 3-D.
points: A point on a plane needs two coordinates; a point in space (a bulb hanging in a room) needs three.
Take three mutually perpendicular lines through a point O: the x-axis, y-axis and z-axis. O is the origin.
The axes determine three coordinate planes: the XY-plane (contains the x- and y-axes), the YZ-plane and the ZX-plane.
The three coordinate planes divide space into eight parts called octants.
Octants are named XOYZ, X′OYZ, X′OY′Z, XOY′Z, XOYZ′, X′OYZ′, X′OY′Z′, XOY′Z′ — numbered I to VIII.

example.q: How many octants, coordinate planes and coordinate axes are there in 3-D space?
steps: Three axes x, y, z through O.
Each pair of axes makes a coordinate plane: XY, YZ, ZX — three planes.
Three planes cut space into 8 octants.

learn.reallife: Air-traffic control at Delhi airport tracks each plane by two ground coordinates plus altitude — a point in 3-D space.

items: Three coordinate planes divide space into 8 octants.

topics.title: Coordinates of a point in space

learn.hook: (2, −3, 5): go 2 along x, 3 backwards along y, 5 up. The signs tell you instantly which octant the point lives in.
points: The coordinates (x, y, z) of P are its (signed) perpendicular distances from the YZ-, ZX- and XY-planes respectively.
On the x-axis: (x, 0, 0); on the y-axis: (0, y, 0); on the z-axis: (0, 0, z). The origin is (0, 0, 0).
In the XY-plane: (x, y, 0); in the YZ-plane: (0, y, z); in the ZX-plane: (x, 0, z).
A point with any coordinate 0 lies on a coordinate plane (or axis), not inside an octant.

topics.title: Distance between two points in space

learn.hook: How long a cable do you need from a ceiling corner to the opposite floor corner? The 3-D distance formula is Pythagoras applied twice.
points: PQ = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)² + (z₂ − z₁)²).
Derivation: draw a box with PQ as a diagonal; Pythagoras in the base gives PN² = (x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)², then PQ² = PN² + (z₂ − z₁)².
Distance from the origin: OP = √(x² + y² + z²).
Collinearity: P, Q, R are collinear if one distance equals the sum of the other two (e.g. PQ + QR = PR).
Syllabus note: the section formula in 3-D is not part of the current rationalised syllabus for this chapter.

example.q: Show that A(1, 2, 3), B(2, 3, 4) and C(4, 5, 6) are collinear.
example.answer: Collinear, with B between A and C

learn.reallife: Architects in Mumbai's high-rises compute diagonal lengths of rooms for cables and ducts using √(l² + b² + h²).

revise.summary: The distance between P(x₁, y₁, z₁) and Q(x₂, y₂, z₂) is √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)² + (z₂ − z₁)²), and from the origin it is √(x² + y² + z²). Three points are collinear if one distance equals the sum of the other two.

Use the space diagonal √(l² + b² + h²) of a box
Test collinearity using PQ + QR = PR
Find an unknown coordinate from a given distance (two answers)

learn.hook: With just the distance formula you can prove a triangle is right-angled, find a missing corner of a parallelogram and even write the equation of a surface.
points: Triangle type: compute all three sides. Right-angled if the squares satisfy Pythagoras; isosceles if two sides are equal; equilateral if all three are equal.
Parallelogram ABCD: opposite sides equal (AB = CD, BC = DA). The missing vertex D = A + C − B (coordinate-wise), since the diagonals bisect each other.
Locus of P equidistant from A and B: PA² = PB²; the squared terms cancel, leaving a plane (the perpendicular bisector plane).
Locus of P with PA + PB = constant 2a (A, B the foci): an ellipsoid. With foci (±c, 0, 0): x²/a² + (y² + z²)/(a² − c²) = 1.
Points on an axis at a given distance: e.g. on the y-axis use (0, y, 0) and solve.

example.q: Find the equation of the set of points P equidistant from A(1, 0, 2) and B(3, 0, 0).
steps: Expand and cancel x², y², z²: −2x + 1 − 4z + 4 = −6x + 9.

learn.hook: A car's speedometer shows 60 km/h at this very instant — but speed is distance over time, and an instant has no time. Calculus resolves this puzzle with limits.
points: Calculus studies how quantities change. Its two pillars are limits and derivatives; derivatives are built from limits.
Average velocity between t₁ and t₂ is [s(t₂) − s(t₁)]/(t₂ − t₁).
For a falling body, s = 4.9t² (metres, seconds). Between t = 2 and t = 2 + h, the average velocity is [4.9(2 + h)² − 4.9 × 4]/h = 19.6 + 4.9h.
As h gets closer and closer to 0, the average velocity gets closer to 19.6 m/s: the instantaneous velocity at t = 2.
In general the derivative is the limiting value of the average rate of change over shrinking intervals.

example.q: For s = 4.9t², find the average velocity from t = 2 s to t = 2.1 s, and guess the velocity at t = 2 s.
steps: Shorter intervals (h = 0.01: 19.649 m/s; h = 0.001: 19.6049 m/s) approach 19.6.
example.answer: 20.09 m/s; instantaneous velocity at t = 2 s is 19.6 m/s

learn.reallife: A cricket speed gun measures the ball's position at tiny time gaps and divides — a real-life version of shrinking the interval h towards 0.

revise.summary: Average velocity is the change in distance divided by the change in time. Instantaneous velocity is the value the average velocity approaches as the time interval shrinks to 0 — the first idea behind the derivative.

Find instantaneous velocity as the limit of average velocities
Explain why we cannot just put h = 0

For s = 4.9t², the average velocity from 2 to 2 + h is 19.6 + 4.9h → 19.6 m/s
Calculus rests on limits and derivatives

Average velocity over an interval is not the same as the velocity at an instant

topics.title: Limits: left, right and from graphs

learn.hook: Walking towards a cliff edge from the left and from the right, do you arrive at the same height? If not, the limit there doesn't exist.
points: lim(x→a) f(x) = l means f(x) gets as close as we like to l when x is close enough to a (x ≠ a).
Left-hand limit (LHL): x → a⁻ (from values below a). Right-hand limit (RHL): x → a⁺ (from above).
The limit exists exactly when LHL and RHL both exist and are equal. The limit may differ from f(a), or exist even if f(a) is undefined.
Tables and graphs: read the values of f(x) as x approaches a from both sides.
For |x|/x: LHL at 0 is −1 and RHL is 1, so lim(x→0) |x|/x does not exist. For [x] at an integer n: LHL = n − 1, RHL = n.

example.q: Let f(x) = x + 2 for x ≤ 1 and f(x) = 3x − 1 for x > 1. Does lim(x→1) f(x) exist?
example.answer: No, the limit does not exist at x = 1

learn.reallife: Income-tax slabs make the tax RATE jump: the rate just below a slab boundary differs from the rate just above it, so the rate function has LHL ≠ RHL at each boundary.

games.title: Does the limit exist?
items: A limit can exist at a point where the function is not defined.
e.g. (x² − 1)/(x − 1) has limit 2 at x = 1 though f(1) is undefined.
If LHL = RHL = 5, the limit is 5.
That is the definition of the limit existing.
The limit ignores the value at a; they may differ.

quiz.q: f(x) = 3x + 2 for x ≤ 0 and 2(x + 1) for x > 0. What is lim(x→0) f(x)?
quiz.explain: LHL = 2 and RHL = 2(0 + 1) = 2; they are equal.
quiz.mistake: Thinks two formulas always mean no limit

quiz.q: What is lim(x→0⁻) |x|/x?
quiz.explain: For x < 0, |x| = −x, so |x|/x = −1.
steps: So the values from the left stay at −1
quiz.mistake: Uses the right-hand value

quiz.q: For f(x) = [x], what is the right-hand limit at x = 3?
quiz.mistake: Gives the left-hand limit 2

quiz.q: For f(x) = [x], does lim(x→3) f(x) exist?
quiz.explain: Just below 3, [x] = 2; just above, [x] = 3.
steps: Answer: No, since LHL = 2 and RHL = 3
quiz.mistake: Uses only f(3)

quiz.q: f(x) = (x² − 4)/(x − 2), x ≠ 2. A table gives f(1.99) = 3.99 and f(2.01) = 4.01. The limit as x → 2 is:
quiz.explain: Both sides approach 4; indeed f(x) = x + 2 for x ≠ 2.
steps: From the left, f(1.99) = 3.99; from the right, f(2.01) = 4.01
quiz.mistake: Thinks the limit cannot exist because f(2) is undefined

quiz.q: f(x) = x² + 1 for x ≤ 1 and 3 − x² for x > 1. What is lim(x→1) f(x)?
quiz.explain: LHL = 1 + 1 = 2 and RHL = 3 − 1 = 2. They agree, so the limit is 2.
quiz.mistake: Uses only one of the two formulas

quiz.q: Which statement about lim(x→a) f(x) is correct?
options: It exists exactly when f(a) is defined
It exists exactly when LHL and RHL exist and are equal
quiz.explain: The value at a itself plays no part in deciding the limit.
steps: The limit depends only on values near a, not at a
It need not equal f(a), and f(a) may be undefined
The test is: both one-sided limits exist and agree
Answer: It exists exactly when LHL and RHL exist and are equal
quiz.mistake: Ties the limit to the function's value at a

quiz.q: f(x) = 5 for x ≠ 2 and f(2) = 7. What is lim(x→2) f(x)?
quiz.explain: Near 2 (but not at 2) the function is 5 on both sides.
steps: For x near 2 but not equal to 2, f(x) = 5
The value f(2) = 7 does not affect the limit
quiz.mistake: Uses the value at the point itself

teach.ask: Gappu thinks the limit at x = a is always f(a). Explain left-hand and right-hand limits and when a limit exists.
teach.praise: Approach from both sides — if they agree, there's a limit, whatever f(a) is. Gappu gets it!
teach.nudge: What must be true about the left and right limits for the limit to exist?

revise.summary: lim(x→a) f(x) = l means f(x) gets as close as we like to l for x near a (x ≠ a). The limit exists exactly when the left-hand and right-hand limits exist and are equal; f(a) itself does not matter.
focus: Find left-hand and right-hand limits of piecewise functions
Decide whether a limit exists by comparing LHL and RHL
Read limits from tables and graphs
Handle |x|/x and [x] near 0 and integers
remember: Limit exists ⇔ LHL and RHL exist and are equal
The limit can differ from f(a), or exist when f(a) is undefined
|x|/x: LHL at 0 = −1, RHL = 1 (no limit); [x] at integer n: LHL = n − 1, RHL = n
traps: Don't use f(a) to decide the limit: look at values near a
For x < 0, |x| = −x, so |x|/x = −1, not 1

topics.title: Algebra of limits; polynomials and rational functions

learn.hook: Most limits in board exams fall in 2 minutes: substitute, and if you get 0/0, factorise and cancel.
points: If lim f = l and lim g = m (as x → a): lim (f ± g) = l ± m, lim fg = lm, lim (f/g) = l/m (m ≠ 0), lim (λf) = λl.
Polynomials: lim(x→a) p(x) = p(a) — just substitute.
Rational function p/q: if q(a) ≠ 0, the limit is p(a)/q(a).
If substitution gives 0/0, factor (x − a) out of the top and bottom, cancel, then substitute.
Example: lim(x→3) (x² − 9)/(x − 3) = lim (x + 3) = 6.

example.q: Evaluate lim(x→2) (x³ − 2x²)/(x² − 4).

learn.reallife: Economists find the marginal cost as a limit of (C(x + h) − C(x))/h; for polynomial cost models the algebra of limits makes this quick.

quiz.q: Evaluate lim(x→3) (5x − 1)/(x + 2).
quiz.explain: The denominator is 5 ≠ 0, so substitute: 14/5.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every limit needs factorising

quiz.q: Evaluate lim(x→5) (x² − 25)/(x − 5).
quiz.mistake: Stops at 0/0

quiz.q: Evaluate lim(x→1) (x² + x − 2)/(x² − 1).
quiz.mistake: Factorises the denominator as (x − 1)²

quiz.q: If lim(x→a) f(x) = 4 and lim(x→a) g(x) = −2, what is lim(x→a) [3f(x) − g(x)]?
steps: lim [3f − g] = 3 lim f − lim g
quiz.mistake: Forgets the double negative

quiz.q: Evaluate lim(x→0) [(x + 1)⁴ − 1]/x.
quiz.explain: Expand: (x + 1)⁴ − 1 = 4x + 6x² + 4x³ + x⁴; divide by x and let x → 0 to get 4.
quiz.mistake: Substitutes and declares 0/0 undefined

quiz.q: Evaluate lim(x→π) (x² − 10).
quiz.explain: A polynomial: substitute x = π. Since π² ≈ 9.87, the answer is a small negative number, not 0.
steps: x² − 10 is a polynomial, so substitute x = π
π² ≈ 9.87, so the value is about −0.13, not 0
quiz.mistake: Treats π² as exactly 10

quiz.q: Evaluate lim(x→3) (x³ − 27)/(x² − 9).
quiz.mistake: Cancels without factoring the cube correctly

quiz.q: Evaluate lim(x→2) (x² − 5x + 6)/(x − 2).
quiz.mistake: Factorises as (x − 2)(x + 3)

teach.ask: Gappu substituted x = 3 into (x² − 9)/(x − 3) and got 0/0, so he wrote 'no limit'. Explain the factor-and-cancel method.
teach.praise: 0/0 is a hint, not a dead end: factor, cancel, substitute. The answer is 6!
teach.nudge: What can you do when direct substitution gives 0/0?

revise.summary: Limits obey sum, difference, product, constant-multiple and quotient rules. For polynomials, substitute; for rational functions, substitute if the denominator is non-zero, and if you get 0/0, factor out (x − a) and cancel first.
focus: Use the algebra of limits
Find limits of polynomials and rational functions by substitution
Remove 0/0 by factorising and cancelling (x − a)
remember: lim (f ± g) = l ± m; lim fg = lm; lim f/g = l/m (m ≠ 0); lim λf = λl
Polynomial: lim(x→a) p(x) = p(a)
0/0 → factor (x − a) from top and bottom, cancel, then substitute
traps: Don't stop at 0/0: it means 'simplify first', not 'the limit is 0'
lim (3f − g) = 3l − m: watch the sign when m is negative

topics.title: The xⁿ limit theorem, rationalising, and unknown constants

learn.hook: One theorem — lim (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) = naⁿ⁻¹ — kills a whole family of limits in a single line.
points: Theorem: for any positive integer n, lim(x→a) (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) = naⁿ⁻¹ (in fact it holds for any rational n with a > 0).
Ratio form: lim(x→1) (xᵐ − 1)/(xⁿ − 1) = m/n (divide top and bottom by x − 1).
Roots: multiply by the conjugate. lim(x→0) (√(1 + x) − 1)/x = lim 1/(√(1 + x) + 1) = 1/2.
Finding a constant: if the limit must exist, make LHL = RHL (for piecewise f) and solve.
Always check the final answer by substitution after simplifying.

example.q: Evaluate lim(x→1) (x⁸ − 1)/(x⁶ − 1).

learn.reallife: Pharmacologists model drug concentration with power functions; the xⁿ limit gives the instantaneous rate of change at any dose.

games.title: Evaluate lim(x→0) (√(1 + x) − 1)/x
items: Multiply top and bottom by √(1 + x) + 1

quiz.q: Evaluate lim(x→2) (x⁵ − 32)/(x − 2).
quiz.mistake: Uses aⁿ instead of aⁿ⁻¹

quiz.q: Evaluate lim(x→1) (x¹² − 1)/(x⁴ − 1).
quiz.mistake: Subtracts the powers

quiz.q: Evaluate lim(x→0) (√(4 + x) − 2)/x.
steps: Multiply top and bottom by √(4 + x) + 2
Numerator: (4 + x) − 4 = x, so the expression = 1/(√(4 + x) + 2)
quiz.mistake: Forgets the +2 in the conjugate

quiz.q: If lim(x→2) (xⁿ − 2ⁿ)/(x − 2) = 80 and n is a positive integer, then n is:
quiz.mistake: Divides 80 by 2

quiz.q: f(x) = kx + 1 for x ≤ 2 and 3x − 1 for x > 2. For which k does lim(x→2) f(x) exist?
quiz.explain: LHL = 2k + 1, RHL = 5. Equal ⇒ k = 2.
quiz.mistake: Equates the coefficients of x

quiz.q: Evaluate lim(x→0) [√(1 + x) − √(1 − x)]/x.
quiz.explain: Multiply by the conjugate: 2x/(x[√(1 + x) + √(1 − x)]) → 2/2 = 1.
steps: Multiply by √(1 + x) + √(1 − x): numerator (1 + x) − (1 − x) = 2x
quiz.mistake: Forgets the factor 2 from (1 + x) − (1 − x)

quiz.q: f(x) = a + 2x for x < 1, 5 at x = 1, b − x for x > 1. If lim(x→1) f(x) = f(1), find a + b.
quiz.explain: LHL = a + 2 = 5 gives a = 3; RHL = b − 1 = 5 gives b = 6. So a + b = 9.
quiz.mistake: Finds only one of the constants

quiz.q: Evaluate lim(x→a) (x^(2/3) − a^(2/3))/(x − a), a > 0.
quiz.explain: The theorem n aⁿ⁻¹ holds for rational n with a > 0: (2/3)a^(−1/3).
steps: The theorem naⁿ⁻¹ holds for rational n when a > 0
quiz.mistake: Forgets to subtract 1 from the power

teach.ask: Gappu must evaluate lim(x→2) (x⁵ − 32)/(x − 2) and lim(x→0) (√(1 + x) − 1)/x. Explain the xⁿ theorem and the rationalisation trick.
must: n times a to the n minus 1
teach.praise: x⁵ − 32 over x − 2 → 5 × 2⁴ = 80, and the conjugate rescues the root limit. Smashing!
teach.nudge: In lim (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a), which formula gives the answer?

revise.summary: lim(x→a) (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) = naⁿ⁻¹, which also gives lim(x→1) (xᵐ − 1)/(xⁿ − 1) = m/n. Limits with square roots are found by multiplying by the conjugate; unknown constants come from making LHL = RHL.
focus: Use the xⁿ theorem and its ratio form m/n
Rationalise with the conjugate to remove 0/0
Find constants that make a limit exist
remember: lim(x→a) (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) = naⁿ⁻¹ (rational n, a > 0)
lim(x→1) (xᵐ − 1)/(xⁿ − 1) = m/n
lim(x→0) (√(1 + x) − 1)/x = 1/2 by the conjugate
traps: The power drops by one: 5 × 2⁴, not 5 × 2⁵
The ratio form gives m/n, not n/m

learn.hook: Type sin(0.001) into a calculator in radian mode: 0.00099999983… Almost exactly 0.001. That's the most famous limit in maths: sin x/x → 1.
points: Sandwich (squeeze) theorem: if g(x) ≤ f(x) ≤ h(x) near a and lim g = lim h = l, then lim f = l.
lim(x→0) sin x/x = 1 (x in radians). Proof: in a unit circle, compare the areas of an inner triangle, a sector and an outer (tangent) triangle to get cos x < sin x/x < 1/cos x, then squeeze.
lim(x→0) (1 − cos x)/x = 0, since (1 − cos x)/x = 2 sin²(x/2)/x = sin(x/2) · [sin(x/2)/(x/2)] → 0 × 1.
Useful forms: sin ax/(bx) → a/b; tan x/x → 1; sin ax/sin bx → a/b.
(cos 2x − 1)/(cos x − 1) = sin²x/sin²(x/2) → 4 as x → 0.

example.q: Evaluate lim(x→0) sin 4x/sin 2x.

learn.reallife: Pendulum clocks rely on sin θ ≈ θ for small angles — the reason small swings take almost the same time.

games.title: Prove lim(x→0) sin x/x = 1 (for 0 < x < π/2)
items: In a unit circle: area of inner triangle < area of sector < area of outer tangent triangle
½ sin x cos x < ½ x < ½ tan x
Divide by ½ sin x (positive): cos x < x/sin x < 1/cos x
Take reciprocals: cos x < sin x/x < 1/cos x
Both bounds tend to 1, so by the sandwich theorem sin x/x → 1

quiz.q: Evaluate lim(x→0) sin 5x/(3x).
quiz.mistake: Inverts the ratio

quiz.q: Evaluate lim(x→0) tan 2x/x.
quiz.explain: tan 2x/x = 2 × [sin 2x/(2x)] × [1/cos 2x] → 2.
quiz.mistake: Treats tan 2x/x like tan x/x = 1

quiz.q: Evaluate lim(x→0) (cos 2x − 1)/(cos x − 1).
quiz.explain: = (−2sin²x)/(−2sin²(x/2)) = [sin x/sin(x/2)]² → (x/(x/2))² = 4.
steps: sin x ≈ x and sin(x/2) ≈ x/2 near 0, so the ratio → (x/(x/2))² = 2²
quiz.mistake: Cancels the cosines directly to get 2

quiz.q: Evaluate lim(x→0) (1 − cos x)/x.
steps: 1 − cos x = 2sin²(x/2), so (1 − cos x)/x = sin(x/2) × [sin(x/2)/(x/2)]
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with lim sin x/x = 1

quiz.q: Evaluate lim(x→0) (1 − cos 2x)/x².
quiz.explain: 1 − cos 2x = 2 sin²x, so the limit is 2[sin x/x]² → 2.
quiz.mistake: Uses 1 − cos 2x = sin²x

quiz.q: Evaluate lim(x→0) sin ax/sin bx (a, b ≠ 0).
quiz.explain: = [sin ax/(ax)] × [(bx)/sin bx] × (a/b) → a/b.
quiz.mistake: Inverts the ratio

quiz.q: The sandwich theorem is used to prove lim sin x/x = 1 because:
options: x is always larger than sin x
sin x/x is squeezed between cos x and 1/cos x, both of which tend to 1
quiz.explain: From cos x < sin x/x < 1/cos x and cos x → 1, the middle function must also tend to 1.
steps: From the areas in the unit circle: cos x < sin x/x < 1/cos x
As x → 0, cos x → 1 and 1/cos x → 1
The middle is squeezed to the same limit
Answer: sin x/x is squeezed between cos x and 1/cos x, both of which tend to 1
quiz.mistake: Thinks 0/0 can be evaluated as 1

quiz.q: Evaluate lim(x→0) (x cos x + sin x)/x.
quiz.explain: = cos x + sin x/x → 1 + 1 = 2.
steps: Split: (x cos x + sin x)/x = cos x + sin x/x
As x → 0: cos x → 1 and sin x/x → 1
quiz.mistake: Forgets the cos x term

teach.ask: Gappu's calculator in radian mode shows sin(0.001)/0.001 ≈ 1. Explain why lim sin x/x = 1 and how to use it for sin 4x/sin 2x.
teach.praise: Squeezed between cos x and 1/cos x, sin x/x has nowhere to go but 1. And matching angles does the rest!
teach.nudge: To use lim sin x/x = 1 for sin 4x, what must the denominator look like?

revise.summary: The key trigonometric limit is lim(x→0) sin x/x = 1 (x in radians), proved with the sandwich theorem; also lim(x→0) (1 − cos x)/x = 0. Rewrite each problem so that sin(ax)/(ax) appears.
focus: Use lim sin x/x = 1 and lim tan x/x = 1 with scaling
Use 1 − cos 2x = 2sin²x and 1 − cos x = 2sin²(x/2)
State the sandwich theorem and how it proves sin x/x → 1
remember: lim(x→0) sin x/x = 1 (x in radians)
lim(x→0) (1 − cos x)/x = 0
sin ax/(bx) → a/b; sin ax/sin bx → a/b; tan x/x → 1
Sandwich: g ≤ f ≤ h and lim g = lim h = l ⇒ lim f = l
traps: sin 5x/(3x) is not 5x/3x by cancelling 'sin': multiply and divide by 5 to get 5/3
(1 − cos x)/x tends to 0, not 1/2; (1 − cos x)/x² tends to 1/2

learn.hook: The steepness of a mountain road at exactly one spot — that's the slope of the tangent, and it's the derivative.
points: Derivative of f at x = a: f′(a) = lim(h→0) [f(a + h) − f(a)]/h, if the limit exists.
The derivative function: f′(x) = lim(h→0) [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h. Notations: f′(x), dy/dx, d/dx f(x), y′.
Using the definition directly is called finding the derivative from first principles.
Results: d/dx(x²) = 2x; d/dx(1/x) = −1/x²; d/dx(√x) = 1/(2√x); d/dx(sin x) = cos x; d/dx(cos x) = −sin x.
Geometric meaning: f′(a) is the slope of the tangent to y = f(x) at (a, f(a)).

example.q: Find the derivative of f(x) = 1/x from first principles.

learn.reallife: ISRO engineers use derivatives of position to get a rocket's instantaneous velocity and acceleration during launch.

games.title: Derivative of sin x from first principles

quiz.q: Using first principles, the derivative of f(x) = 3x² − 4x at x = 2 is:
quiz.mistake: Uses f(2) = 4 as the derivative

quiz.q: What is the slope of the tangent to y = x² at x = 3?
quiz.explain: dy/dx = 2x = 6 at x = 3.
quiz.mistake: Gives the y-value 9

quiz.q: Which limit defines f′(a)?
quiz.explain: It is the limit of the average rate of change as h → 0.
steps: f′(a) is the limit of the average rate [f(a + h) − f(a)]/h
The interval h must shrink to 0
h → ∞ or a '+' sign would be wrong
quiz.mistake: Lets h tend to infinity

quiz.q: From first principles, d/dx(√x) is:
quiz.mistake: Forgets the factor 2

quiz.q: The derivative of a constant function f(x) = 7 is:
quiz.explain: f(x + h) − f(x) = 0 for all h, so the limit is 0.
steps: f(x + h) − f(x) = 7 − 7 = 0 for every h
quiz.mistake: Thinks the derivative of a constant is the constant

quiz.q: For f(x) = 1/x, what is f′(2)?
quiz.mistake: Forgets the minus sign

quiz.q: From first principles, d/dx(x³) is:
quiz.explain: [(x + h)³ − x³]/h = 3x² + 3xh + h² → 3x².
quiz.mistake: Integrates instead of differentiating

quiz.q: The derivative of f(x) = x at x = 5 is:
quiz.explain: [(5 + h) − 5]/h = 1 for every h ≠ 0.
quiz.mistake: Gives f(5) instead of f′(5)

teach.ask: Gappu wants to know the steepness of y = x² at x = 3, exactly. Explain the first-principles definition of the derivative and what it means on a graph.
teach.praise: The derivative is the limiting slope as h shrinks — the slope of the tangent. At x = 3 it's 6!
teach.nudge: What happens to h in the definition, and what does the answer represent on the graph?

revise.summary: The derivative of f at a is f′(a) = lim(h→0) [f(a + h) − f(a)]/h, the slope of the tangent at (a, f(a)). Using this definition directly is called finding the derivative from first principles.
focus: Find derivatives of x², x³, 1/x, √x and constants from first principles
Find f′(a) at a point and interpret it as a tangent slope
Recognise the notations f′(x), dy/dx and y′
remember: f′(a) = lim(h→0) [f(a + h) − f(a)]/h
d/dx(sin x) = cos x; d/dx(cos x) = −sin x
f′(a) = slope of the tangent to y = f(x) at (a, f(a))
traps: The limit is as h → 0, not h → ∞
The derivative of a constant is 0, not the constant itself

learn.hook: Nobody differentiates (x⁵ + 3x² − 7)(x² + 1) from first principles in an exam. A handful of rules does it in seconds.
points: Sum/difference: (u ± v)′ = u′ ± v′. Constant multiple: (cu)′ = cu′.
Product (Leibnitz) rule: (uv)′ = u′v + uv′.
Quotient rule: (u/v)′ = (u′v − uv′)/v², v ≠ 0.
Power rule: d/dx(xⁿ) = nxⁿ⁻¹ for every positive integer n (proved using the binomial theorem). So d/dx(aₙxⁿ + … + a₁x + a₀) = naₙxⁿ⁻¹ + … + a₁.
Syllabus note: the chain rule is only assessed formatively in this chapter; expand composite expressions instead (e.g. (2x + 1)² = 4x² + 4x + 1).

example.q: Differentiate y = (x² + 1)(x³ − 2x).
steps: u = x² + 1, u′ = 2x; v = x³ − 2x, v′ = 3x² − 2.

learn.reallife: An e-commerce startup's revenue R(p) = p × demand(p); the product rule gives the marginal revenue that pricing teams track.

quiz.q: d/dx(x⁷) is:
quiz.explain: nxⁿ⁻¹ with n = 7.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to reduce the power

quiz.q: Differentiate f(x) = 4x³ − 3x² + 2x − 5 and find f′(1).
steps: f′(x) = 12x² − 6x + 2 (power rule term by term; constant → 0)
quiz.mistake: Keeps the constant −5 in the derivative

quiz.q: Using the product rule, d/dx[(x + 2)(x − 3)] is:
steps: Product rule: (uv)′ = u′v + uv′ with u = x + 2, v = x − 3
quiz.mistake: Multiplies the derivatives (1 × 1 = 1)

quiz.q: Using the quotient rule, d/dx[x/(x + 1)] is:
steps: Quotient rule with u = x, v = x + 1: u′ = 1, v′ = 1
quiz.mistake: Reverses the order in the numerator

quiz.q: If y = (2x + 1)², find dy/dx at x = 1 by expanding first.
quiz.mistake: Gives 2(2x + 1) = 6, forgetting the factor 2 from inside

quiz.q: The derivative of f(x) = 1 + x + x²/2 + x³/3 at x = 1 is:
quiz.mistake: Computes f(1) instead

quiz.q: Which is the product (Leibnitz) rule?
quiz.explain: Each factor is differentiated in turn while the other is kept.
steps: Product rule: differentiate each factor in turn, keeping the other
The minus sign and the /v² belong to the quotient rule
quiz.mistake: Multiplies the two derivatives

quiz.q: For f(x) = x¹⁰⁰ + x⁹⁹ + … + x + 1, what is f′(1)?
quiz.mistake: Counts the terms instead of adding the powers

teach.ask: Gappu must differentiate (x² + 1)(x³ − 2x) and x/(x + 1). Explain the product rule, the quotient rule and the power rule.
teach.praise: Power rule for each term, product rule for products, quotient rule for fractions. Differentiation dojo complete!
teach.nudge: In the quotient rule, what goes in the denominator?

revise.summary: Derivatives follow simple rules: (u ± v)′ = u′ ± v′, (cu)′ = cu′, the product rule (uv)′ = u′v + uv′, the quotient rule (u/v)′ = (u′v − uv′)/v², and the power rule d/dx(xⁿ) = nxⁿ⁻¹.
focus: Differentiate polynomials term by term with the power rule
Use the product rule and quotient rule
Expand simple composite expressions before differentiating
Evaluate a derivative at a point
remember: d/dx(xⁿ) = nxⁿ⁻¹
(uv)′ = u′v + uv′
traps: (uv)′ is not u′v′: differentiate one factor at a time
In the quotient rule the order matters: u′v − uv′, not uv′ − u′v

topics.title: Derivatives of trigonometric functions and mixed problems

learn.hook: Sine becomes cosine, cosine becomes minus sine, tangent becomes sec². With the product and quotient rules, every trig derivative is within reach.
points: d/dx(sin x) = cos x; d/dx(cos x) = −sin x; d/dx(tan x) = sec²x (from tan x = sin x/cos x and the quotient rule).
d/dx(sec x) = sec x tan x; d/dx(cosec x) = −cosec x cot x; d/dx(cot x) = −cosec²x.
Products and quotients: e.g. d/dx[x⁴(5 sin x − 3 cos x)] = 4x³(5 sin x − 3 cos x) + x⁴(5 cos x + 3 sin x).
Linear fractions: d/dx[(ax + b)/(cx + d)] = (ad − bc)/(cx + d)².
Simplify with identities before or after differentiating, e.g. sin²x + cos²x = 1.

example.q: Find the derivative of tan x using the quotient rule.
steps: (cos x · cos x − sin x · (−sin x))/cos²x.

learn.reallife: Wave and vibration analysis in civil engineering (bridges, metro tracks) differentiates sine and cosine terms to find velocities and accelerations.

games.title: Differentiate sec x = 1/cos x

learn.hook: Two batters both average 50. One scores 48, 50, 52 every match; the other scores 0, 100, 0, 100. Same mean — very different reliability. That difference is dispersion.
points: Statistics collects, organises and interprets data. Mean, median and mode (from Class 10) are measures of central tendency: they give a typical value.
Data sets with the same mean can be spread very differently, so we also need measures of dispersion.
Dispersion is the scatter (variability) of observations about a central value.
Measures of dispersion: range, quartile deviation, mean deviation and standard deviation (with variance).
Range = maximum value − minimum value. It is quick but uses only the two extreme values.

learn.hook: How far, on average, is each score from the centre? Take the distances (ignoring direction) and average them — that's the mean deviation.
points: Deviations xᵢ − a from a central value a can be positive or negative; about the mean they add up to 0. So we use absolute values |xᵢ − a|.
Mean deviation about a: M.D.(a) = (1/n) Σ |xᵢ − a|. Usually a is the mean or the median.
About the mean: find x̄, then the absolute deviations, then their average.
About the median: arrange the data, find the median M, then (1/n) Σ |xᵢ − M|.
Mean deviation about the median is never more than mean deviation about the mean.

points: Discrete frequency distribution: x̄ = Σfᵢxᵢ/N where N = Σfᵢ; M.D.(x̄) = (1/N) Σ fᵢ|xᵢ − x̄|.

topics.title: Grouped median, M.D. about the median, and limitations

learn.hook: For a big class table, the median isn't a value you can just spot — it's found with a formula, and then you measure spread around it.
points: Median of grouped data: find N/2, locate the median class (first cumulative frequency ≥ N/2).
Median = l + [(N/2 − C)/f] × h, where l = lower limit of the median class, C = cumulative frequency before it, f = its frequency, h = class width.
M.D. about the median = (1/N) Σ fᵢ|xᵢ − M|, using class marks xᵢ.
Limitations of M.D.: absolute values are awkward to handle algebraically; it is not well suited to further statistical work.
Also, if the data are very variable, the median is not a good representative, and the sum of absolute deviations about the mean is larger than about the median, so the choice of centre matters.

topics.title: Variance and standard deviation for raw data

learn.hook: Squaring deviations removes the sign problem AND gives a measure with beautiful algebra. That's why standard deviation rules statistics.
points: Squaring deviations makes them non-negative and avoids absolute values. Variance σ² = (1/n) Σ (xᵢ − x̄)², the mean of squared deviations.
Standard deviation σ = +√(variance). It has the same units as the data.
Shortcut: σ² = (1/n)Σxᵢ² − (x̄)² = [nΣxᵢ² − (Σxᵢ)²]/n².
σ = 0 exactly when all observations are equal.
Syllabus note: analysis of frequency distributions using the coefficient of variation is not part of the current rationalised syllabus for this chapter.

topics.title: Variance and SD for frequency distributions

learn.hook: Thousands of exam scores in a table? Use frequencies, class marks and the step-deviation shortcut — and SD comes out cleanly.
points: Discrete: σ² = (1/N) Σ fᵢ(xᵢ − x̄)², N = Σfᵢ.
Continuous: use class marks as xᵢ, same formula.
Shortcut: σ² = (1/N)Σfᵢxᵢ² − x̄², or σ = (1/N)√(NΣfᵢxᵢ² − (Σfᵢxᵢ)²).

learn.hook: Before a cricket toss, everyone knows the possible outcomes — heads or tails — but no one knows which. That's a random experiment, and probability measures our uncertainty about it.
points: A random experiment has more than one possible outcome, and the outcome cannot be predicted in advance. The set of all outcomes is the sample space S.

Classical probability: P(E) = (number of favourable outcomes)/(total number of outcomes), when all outcomes are equally likely. It fails when outcomes are not equally likely or infinitely many, which is why we need the axiomatic approach.
An event is a subset of the sample space. E.g. 'an even number' on a die is E = {2, 4, 6} ⊆ S = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}.
The event E occurs if the actual outcome ω belongs to E.
Toss a coin twice: S = {HH, HT, TH, TT}; 'exactly one head' = {HT, TH}.

topics.title: Impossible, sure, simple, compound and complementary events

learn.hook: Rolling a 7 on a normal die can never happen; rolling a number below 7 always happens. Events come in types, and naming them makes problems easy.
points: Impossible event: ∅ (no outcome), e.g. 'a 7 on a die'. Sure event: S itself, e.g. 'a number less than 7'.
Simple (elementary) event: exactly one sample point, e.g. {4}.
Compound event: more than one sample point, e.g. 'an even number' = {2, 4, 6}.
Complementary event 'not A': A′ = S − A = {ω ∈ S : ω ∉ A}.
Example: for a die, if A = {1, 2, 3}, then A′ = {4, 5, 6}.

topics.title: Algebra of events: or, and, but not

learn.hook: 'Rain OR wind', 'rain AND wind', 'rain but NOT wind' — event language is set language in disguise.
points: 'A or B' = A ∪ B (at least one of them occurs). 'A and B' = A ∩ B (both occur).
'A but not B' = A − B = A ∩ B′.
A and B are mutually exclusive if A ∩ B = ∅: they cannot occur together.
E₁, E₂, …, Eₙ are exhaustive if E₁ ∪ E₂ ∪ … ∪ Eₙ = S. If, in addition, they are pairwise disjoint, they are mutually exclusive and exhaustive.
Example with one die: A = {1, 3, 5} (odd) and B = {2, 4, 6} (even) are mutually exclusive and exhaustive.

topics.title: Axioms of probability and equally likely outcomes

learn.hook: Kolmogorov boiled all of probability down to three simple rules. Every formula you'll use follows from them.
points: Axiom 1: P(E) ≥ 0 for every event E. Axiom 2: P(S) = 1. Axiom 3: if E and F are mutually exclusive, P(E ∪ F) = P(E) + P(F).
Consequences: P(∅) = 0, and 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1.
For a finite sample space, assign P(ωᵢ) to each outcome with 0 ≤ P(ωᵢ) ≤ 1 and ΣP(ωᵢ) = 1. P(E) = sum of P(ωᵢ) over ωᵢ ∈ E.
An assignment is valid only if every value is between 0 and 1 and the values add up to 1.
If all n outcomes are equally likely, each has probability 1/n and P(E) = n(E)/n(S).

topics.title: Addition rule and the complement rule

points: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B) for any events A and B.
If A and B are mutually exclusive, P(A ∩ B) = 0, so P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B).
Complement rule: P(not A) = P(A′) = 1 − P(A).
P(A but not B) = P(A) − P(A ∩ B). P(neither A nor B) = P(A′ ∩ B′) = 1 − P(A ∪ B).
Draw a Venn diagram: the three regions A only, both, B only add to P(A ∪ B).

example.q: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.3 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.1. Find P(A ∪ B), P(A′ ∩ B′) and P(A but not B).

quiz.q: If P(A) = 0.6, P(B) = 0.5 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.3, find P(A ∪ B).
steps: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)
quiz.mistake: Adds without subtracting the overlap

quiz.q: A and B are mutually exclusive with P(A) = 1/4 and P(B) = 1/3. What is P(A ∪ B)?
quiz.explain: For mutually exclusive events, add: 1/4 + 1/3 = 7/12.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies the probabilities

quiz.mistake: Gives the same probability

steps: Rearrange the addition rule: P(A ∩ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∪ B)
