quiz.mistake: Computes 1 − P(A ∩ B)

quiz.q: Two dice are thrown. What is the probability that the sum is NOT 7?
steps: Sum 7 occurs in 6 of 36 outcomes: P = 1/6
quiz.mistake: Forgets the complement rule

quiz.q: Can P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.7 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.1 be valid probabilities?
options: Yes, all values are between 0 and 1
Yes, since P(A) + P(B) > 1 is allowed for mutually exclusive events
No, since P(A ∪ B) would be 1.1 > 1
No, since P(A ∩ B) must be 0
quiz.explain: P(A ∪ B) = 0.5 + 0.7 − 0.1 = 1.1, which exceeds 1.
steps: Answer: No, since P(A ∪ B) would be 1.1 > 1
quiz.mistake: Checks only the individual values

teach.ask: Gappu added P(king) and P(heart) and got 17/52. Explain the addition rule, when you can simply add, and the complement rule.
teach.praise: Add, then subtract the overlap — unless the events can't happen together. And not-A is 1 minus A. Deal me in!
teach.nudge: Which card did Gappu count twice?

revise.summary: For any events, P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B); for mutually exclusive events the last term is 0. The complement rule P(A′) = 1 − P(A) gives 'not' and 'neither' probabilities quickly.
focus: Use the addition rule for overlapping events
Use P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) for mutually exclusive events
Use the complement rule, including P(neither A nor B) = 1 − P(A ∪ B)
Check whether given probabilities are consistent
remember: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)
P(A but not B) = P(A) − P(A ∩ B); P(A′ ∩ B′) = 1 − P(A ∪ B)
traps: Don't forget to subtract the overlap P(A ∩ B) for overlapping events
Values between 0 and 1 can still be inconsistent if P(A ∪ B) comes out above 1

learn.hook: What are your chances of winning a lottery where you pick 6 numbers from 20? About 1 in 38,760. Combinations turn probability into counting.
points: P(E) = n(E)/n(S), where both counts are found with permutations or combinations.
Selections (committees, hands of cards, balls drawn together): use ⁿCᵣ for both n(E) and n(S).
Arrangements (letters, seating): use factorials or ⁿPᵣ for both counts.
'At least one' problems: P = 1 − P(none).
Read carefully whether order matters and whether drawing is with or without replacement.

example.q: A committee of 3 is chosen from 4 men and 6 women. Find the probability that it has exactly 2 women.

learn.reallife: State lotteries publish the odds 1/ⁿCᵣ; a lottery picking 6 of 20 numbers gives 1/38,760 — counting tells you the real chance.

quiz.q: Two balls are drawn together from a bag of 5 red and 3 blue balls. What is the probability that both are blue?
quiz.explain: ³C₂/⁸C₂ = 3/28.
steps: Favourable: choose 2 of the 3 blue: ³C₂ = 3
quiz.mistake: Uses draws with replacement (3/8)²

quiz.q: A letter is chosen at random from the word MATHEMATICS. What is the probability that it is M?
quiz.explain: There are 11 letters, two of which are M.
quiz.mistake: Counts distinct letters (8) as the total

quiz.q: The letters of MONDAY are arranged at random. What is the probability that the two vowels are together?
steps: Vowels O, A as one block: 5! × 2! = 120 × 2 = 240
quiz.mistake: Forgets to arrange the vowels inside the block

quiz.q: 4 cards are drawn from a deck. What is the probability that all are spades?
quiz.explain: Choose 4 of the 13 spades out of all 4-card hands.
steps: Favourable: 4 of the 13 spades → ¹³C₄; total: any 4 of 52 → ⁵²C₄
quiz.mistake: Treats the draws as independent with replacement

quiz.q: In a lottery, 6 different numbers are chosen from 1 to 20 (order does not matter). The chance of winning with one ticket is 1/N. What is N?
quiz.explain: N = ²⁰C₆ = 38,760 equally likely choices, one of which wins.
steps: Order does not matter, so count selections
quiz.mistake: Uses ²⁰P₆ = 27,907,200, treating order as important

quiz.q: A committee of 2 is chosen from 3 boys and 2 girls. What is the probability that at least one girl is chosen?
quiz.explain: P(no girl) = ³C₂/⁵C₂ = 3/10, so P(at least one girl) = 7/10.
steps: P(at least one girl) = 1 − P(no girl)
quiz.mistake: Gives P(no girl)

quiz.q: Three cards are drawn together from a deck. The probability that all are kings is 1/k. What is k?
quiz.mistake: Uses (4/52)³ = 1/2197, treating the draws as with replacement

quiz.q: 6 boys and 4 girls stand in a row at random. What is the probability that a particular boy stands at the left end?
quiz.explain: Any of the 10 people is equally likely to be at the left end.
steps: All 10 people are equally likely to be at the left end
quiz.mistake: Divides by the number of boys only

teach.ask: Gappu wants the chance that a 3-person committee from 4 men and 6 women has exactly 2 women. Explain how to use combinations for probability.
teach.praise: Count favourable choices, count all choices, divide. 60 out of 120 — a half! Counting powers probability.
teach.nudge: How do you count the total number of possible committees?

revise.summary: Many probability problems are counting problems: P(E) = n(E)/n(S), with both counts found by combinations (selections) or permutations (arrangements). For 'at least one', use 1 − P(none).
focus: Count n(E) and n(S) with ⁿCᵣ for selections
Count with factorials or ⁿPᵣ for arrangements
Use 1 − P(none) for 'at least one' problems
Decide whether order matters
remember: P(E) = n(E)/n(S)
Selections (committees, hands, balls drawn together): ⁿCᵣ
Arrangements (letters, seating): factorials or ⁿPᵣ
P(at least one) = 1 − P(none)
traps: Use the same method (both combinations or both arrangements) for n(E) and n(S)
Don't mix ⁿPᵣ in the numerator with ⁿCᵣ in the denominator
